title: How Russia's ballistic missiles, jet-powered drones have kept Ukraine under pressure
text: Smoke rises in the aftermath of a Russian jet-powered drone strike, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Kyiv, Ukraine, September 28, 2026. Russia launched ballistic missiles and several jet-powered drones at Kyiv, Ukraine's air force reported on Tuesday, as Moscow tries to force Ukraine to crumble under round-the-clock bombardment of its capital and other cities. The assaults have involved new jet-powered drones that fly too quickly and too high for Ukraine's ground-based air defences to bring down. Kyiv is racing to keep up by developing faster interceptor drones. "Russia's terror against Ukraine is intensifying by the day," Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha said on X. "This is Russia's deliberate escalation instead of accepting Ukraine's offers to cease fire, negotiate and end the war," he added. Russian ballistic missiles have also penetrated Ukrainian defences, because the country is critically short of US-made Patriot interceptor missiles. Watch Russia Bombards Ukraine Capital, Other Cities With Jet-Powered Drones; Dozens Killed & Injured Ukraine has been dependent on American supplies of Patriot air defence systems, but its stockpiles are running low due to the war in Iran, leaving the country vulnerable to Russian attacks. According to AP, Ukraine has received only limited quantities of Patriot missiles this year, despite President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's appeals. Russia's defence ministry said its forces struck data processing centres in Kyiv which, it claims, serve the Ukrainian military, an army that is making growing use of artificial intelligence on the battlefield. The ministry also listed other targets: sites in the capital and the Kyiv region where drones and cruise missiles were kept, along with an electrical substation, a drone manufacturing facility and port infrastructure in the southern Odesa region. However, Ukraine has not simply endured the Russian barrage. Its long-range drones have hit Russian missile and drone factories and launch sites, as well as oil refineries, which has led to fuel shortages. Europe seeks self-sufficiency In late August, the UK government agreed to allow defence company MBDA to declassify information on British-made components used in the Scalp missile, the French version of the UK's Storm Shadow cruise missile. The move enabled Ukraine and France to work towards establishing assembly lines in Ukraine and allow Kyiv to produce the long-range weapon domestically. The Scalp missiles are expected to serve as alternatives to the American Patriots, as Europe tries to overcome its dependence on the US for its defence. British PM Andy Burnham said the allies were doing "everything we can" to support Ukraine, including drawing from their own air defence stocks and helping other countries do the same. "This is the moment to keep up the pressure on Russia, the moment to squeeze their ability to fund this illegal war," he said, while chairing his first meeting of the âcoalition of the willingâ group, in late August. title: Moscow vows to step up strikes on Ukraine as Zelenskyy threatens to attack more Russian refineries
text: Moscow vows tougher strikes on Ukraine Russia will intensify strikes on Kyiv and other regions of Ukraine following recent remarks by president Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the Russian defence ministry said on Sunday. The remarks came as Moscow warned of a further escalation in the aerial war after Kyiv threatened to expand attacks on Russian oil refineries. The ministry, cited by Russia's state-run TASS news agency, said that the Russian forces would step up attacks on military facilities, defence industry sites and related infrastructure in Kyiv and elsewhere in Ukraine. The warning followed remarks by Zelenskiy to Reuters that Ukraine would "double down" on attacks against Russian oil refineries in response to what he described as a new Russian campaign targeting infrastructure across Ukrainian cities. Zelenskyy said Ukrainian intelligence had obtained documents indicating that Russian president Vladimir Putin had approved a broader range of targets ahead of the winter campaign. "We saw documents and we know that they allow them to attack infrastructure, logistics, and especially to attack in the cities, in the villages, everywhere, roads, schools, hospitals," Zelenskyy told Reuters. "To pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities: this is the goal of the operation," he said. Zelenskiy said Ukraine would respond by targeting Russian energy infrastructure but would not deliberately attack civilian facilities. "We have to respond in any way we can. With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refiners etc: what gives money to them for this war," he said. "But we will not respond, of course, just like them, on any civilian objects." The latest warning came as attacks on energy, transport and communications infrastructure intensified. Russian drones and missiles have struck targets across Ukraine, while Kyiv has increasingly targeted Russia's oil industry, which it says helps finance Moscow's war effort. On Sunday, a fire broke out at an industrial site in Russia's Krasnodar region after falling drone debris struck the facility in the Temryuk district, regional authorities said. Three people were injured and taken for medical treatment. Meanwhile, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in Kyiv on Sunday in a show of support for Ukraine. Merz said Germany would continue backing Kyiv and warned of the wider consequences of Russia's war. "If Russia is not stopped, sooner or later its war machine will turn against us," Merz said. "You can continue to count on our help." Zelenskiy thanked Germany on X, saying the two countries would make "important agreements" to strengthen Ukraine's defences. title: $26,000 to fight for Russia: How Moscow recruits Americans via TikTok and Telegram
text: File photo: Russian President Vladimir Putin arrives for a wreath-laying ceremony surrounded by Russian military personnels Russia is increasingly turning to foreign recruits to replenish its forces fighting in Ukraine, with at least 18 Americans identified as having joined the Russian military, according to Ukrainian officials cited by the New York Post. US recruits are reportedly being offered a signing bonus of about $26,000, along with a monthly salary. The recruitment is being driven through a network of agents who use platforms including Facebook, TikTok and Telegram to find potential recruits. Ukrainian officials said recruiters can earn money for each person they bring in, with some reportedly receiving about $24,000 per recruit as well as a share of the recruitâs salary. The effort extends far beyond Americans. Ukrainian security officials have identified nearly 29,000 foreigners from 135 countries fighting for Russia, although the actual number could be higher. Amnesty International has separately documented deceptive and exploitative recruitment practices targeting foreign nationals, including promises of civilian jobs, high salaries, legal status or Russian citizenship. US citizens joining Russia's war One of those recruited was Seth William Baker, a former US Marine from Gilbert, Arizona. Baker, who had served as a lance corporal and worked as a bulk fuel specialist, was 23 when he was killed on the frontlines in Ukraine, around three months after signing up. Baker had joined the Marines at 18 but was later discharged after refusing the military's Covid-19 vaccine mandate. He subsequently became involved with Russian propaganda online before travelling to Russia. In a recording made from a Russian bunker, Baker said the vaccine mandate had been one of the factors behind his decision to leave the US military and join Russia's war effort. Vitaliy Matvienko, who heads Ukraine's state-backed project encouraging Russian soldiers to surrender, described Baker's case as typical of the people Russia's recruitment network seeks out. He said Russia had turned foreign recruitment into an âentire industryâ as it struggles to replace battlefield losses. Baker is not the only American identified as having fought for Russia. Michael Gloss, 21, the son of a former CIA official, was killed while fighting in Ukraine in April 2024. Ukrainian intelligence has also identified 17 other Americans who had enlisted in the Russian military. Another case involves former Massachusetts city councillor Wilmer Puello-Mota, who left the US while facing a child sexual-abuse-related case and later joined Russian forces. He was wounded by shrapnel in Ukraine in August. Derek Huffman, 47, moved his family to Russia and later signed up for the military, according to the report. He had previously criticised what he described as LGBTQ âindoctrinationâ in the US and said he wanted to earn respect and Russian citizenship. Matvienko said foreign recruits serve a dual purpose for Moscow: they provide additional manpower while also allowing Russia to portray Americans and other foreigners fighting alongside its troops as evidence of international support for its war. Foreign recruits can also be easier for Russia to absorb politically when they are killed, he said, because their deaths do not necessarily generate the same reaction inside Russian society as the deaths of Russian soldiers. The recruitment comes as Russia continues to sustain heavy battlefield losses. Ukrainian officials cited by the New York Post estimated that Russia was suffering tens of thousands of casualties each month and increasingly relying on foreign nationals to help fill its ranks. title: Russia strikes Ukraine's largest mobile service provider; why communication networks matter in war
text: âSmoke rises over the headquarters of Kyivstar, one of Ukraine's largest telecoms companies, hit by a Russian jet drone strike (Reuters) Russia struck the headquarters of Kyivstar, Ukraineâs largest mobile service provider, in Kyiv on Sunday, in the latest attack on the countryâs communications infrastructure. Kyivstar confirmed that its head office was hit and said there were no casualties. According to Reuters, the strike came as Moscow continued attacks on Ukrainian data centres and communications infrastructure. Russiaâs defence ministry said it had struck a Vodafone Ukraine data centre, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a Kyiv data centre was hit twice, wounding two children and an adult. Russia Pounds Kharkiv As EU Warns Of More Russian Attacks | Watch Russia had already been stepping up strikes on Ukraineâs data centres and telecommunications infrastructure in the days before the Kyivstar attack On September 23, Russian strikes damaged facilities used by several internet providers in Kyiv, disrupting internet services for around 100,000 households in Kyiv and the surrounding region, according to Ukraineâs digital transformation ministry. According to Ukrainian companies and officials, infrastructure belonging to providers including Domonet, Kievnet and Faust was damaged, while a data centre housing infrastructure for hosting provider MiroHost was destroyed. A Russian strike also damaged a Datagroup data centre in Kyiv, further disrupting Ukraineâs digital infrastructure. Russian defence ministry said the strikes included data-processing and telecommunications centres such as New-Telco and United DC, claiming they were linked to Ukrainian military communications and intelligence. Moscow also said the Datagroup facility was being used by Ukrainian military intelligence. Why Ukraineâs communications network matters in the war Ukraineâs communications infrastructure has become an increasingly important part of its war effort, connecting military units, command centres and battlefield systems while also carrying information used for air-raid and missile alerts. Ukraine foreign minister Andrii Sybiha said Russia was targeting major Ukrainian data centres in an attempt to disrupt the flow of information, while stressing that rapid missile and drone alerts are crucial for saving lives. As the war has become increasingly dependent on drones, real-time intelligence and networked command systems, reliable digital connectivity has become critical to the speed at which information moves from the battlefield to commanders and frontline forces. Ukraineâs military also relies on digital platforms to build a real-time picture of the battlefield. Systems such as Delta combine information from multiple sources to help commanders track Russian forces, monitor battlefield developments and coordinate operations

title: Ukraine debuts ballistic missile FP-7 as Kyiv faces ammunition shortages
text: "Next up: production", Zelensky said. Ukraine on Thursday deployed its home-built ballistic missile "FP-7" in combat for the first time, amid increasing ballistic and jet-powered attacks on Kyiv. Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky informed of the deployment through his post on X. "Ukrainian tactical ballistic missile. FP-7. First combat use. Thank you for the result", Zelensky wrote on X "Next up: production", he added. Zelensky's remarks came as Kyiv conducted deep strikes inside Russian territory. Ukrainian strikes hit a vessel in the Black Sea, an oil facility in Samara, and a supply depot in the Bryansk region. A site in the Oryol region was also hit, which Zelensky said was "used to launch and store attack drones". What is FP-7? FP-7 is a ground-based ballistic missile developed by Ukrainian defence firm Fire Point. According to the defence firm, it has been designed to deliver a payload weighing up to 200 kilograms and can engage targets at ranges of up to 250 kilometres. The missile has a maximum speed of up to 5400 kilometres per hour, and boasts a target accuracy of around 14 metres. It can reach a maximum altitude of up to 60 kilometres and has a maximum flight time of five minutes. The launch system uses a ground-based platform, which offers considerable strategic flexibility, mobility, and the capacity for rapid deployment. Thanks to this design, the system can be adjusted to shifting mission demands and a variety of operational scenarios. The missile is under development as a ballistic interceptor for the "Freyja" program. Until it is fully integrated into the system, it is regarded as an affordable alternative to the American supersonic Army Tactical Missile System (ATACMS). Ukraine is currently short of ammunition, with the stock significantly declining amid escalated exchange of airstrikes with Russia. "The Ministry of foreign affairs, the ministry of defense, and the office team will conduct an immediate review of the agreements reached with our partners on providing F-16s with the necessary ammunition", Zelensky said. In another post, Zelensky thanked people working in the defence industry for ensuring that Ukraine has means to respond to Russian attacks. "I thank all our defenders who are working to send Russiaâs sick war back to where it came from", he said, adding that Ukraine "will continue to deprive Russia of the ability to keep this war going". On Wednesday, Russia conducted one of its biggest drone and missile attacks on Kyiv's power grid and areas around the region, leaving seven people dead, officials said. According to the AP, the assault caused massive power cuts and raised questions over whether it signalled the start of Russia's expected cold-weather offensive, which Ukrainian officials characterise as an attempt to "weaponise winter".

title: Lithuania airport shut, Nato jets scramble as 'drone spotted' along Belarus border
text: Authorities advised residents in the Vilnius region to be prepared to seek shelter if necessary, it said. Vilnius airport in Lithuania was temporarily closed and Nato air-policing fighter jets were scrambled after a possible drone was detected flying from the direction of Belarus, Lithuania's National Crisis Control Centre told news agency Reuters. Authorities advised residents in the Vilnius region to be prepared to seek shelter if necessary, it said. The incident comes as security concerns continue to rise across the Baltic region, where countries bordering or located near Russia and Belarus have reported a growing number of airspace incidents linked to the war in Ukraine. Lithuania is a Nato and European Union (EU) member and has been closely monitoring developments along its borders amid concerns about possible Russian aggression. Russia has rejected allegations that it is planning an attack on Nato, while Western officials have said Moscow does not currently have the capability for a direct assault. The development unflods as neighbouring Latvia prepares for a parliamentary election on Saturday, with security concerns featuring prominently in the campaign. Opinion polls have placed Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs' centrist United List at around 14%, narrowly ahead of the overtly pro-Russian Sovereign Power. However, political fragmentation could make it difficult to form a government after the election. Kulbergs, a 47-year-old businessman and amateur rally driver, took office in May after the previous coalition collapsed over its handling of incidents involving military drones that entered Latvian airspace without being detected. The drones were Ukrainian, although Latvian officials blamed Russia for causing them to stray from their intended flight paths. The incident in Lithuania is likely to add to security concerns across the Baltics, where governments have remained on alert over airspace violations and the wider regional impact of the Russia-Ukraine war. title: Zelenskyy, at UN, urges leaders to keep choking Russia's revenues and impede its war efforts
text: Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy speaks during the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly at United Nations headquarters. (AP photo) Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told world leaders Wednesday that Vladimir Putin is the only obstacle to ending "the ridiculous and never-ending war," and he urged nations large and small to pressure the Russian president for peace by choking the country's revenues and impeding its war efforts. "Our target is Russia's ability to finance this war, to drag it out, to make it more brutal and more destructive," Zelenskyy told the U.N. General Assembly's annual global gathering. "Russia's finances and Russia's production are what must be stopped if Putin is to be stopped." Watch 'WHY NOT STOP ZELENSKY?': Putin Aide RIPS West's Hypocrisy On Ukraine's Attacks On Nuclear Plant When Russia gets money from trade, "it always says no to diplomacy," Zelenskyy argued, "so Russia's revenues must remain a target." Earlier Wednesday, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov clashed with Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha and her country's European supporters at a UN Security Council meeting, and Lavrov and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio met on the assembly sidelines and discussed the war. Top US diplomat talks about potential for a ceasefire Rubio later told reporters that Russia and Ukraine have expressed interest in a limited ceasefire that would halt attacks on grain shipments - both countries are major exporters -- and on each country's energy sectors, which have been targeted in escalating drone and missile attacks. Watch Zelenskyâs âNon-Stop Sniffingâ Caught On Cam; Web Erupts Over Nose-Touching Rubio said reaching even a partial deal would be difficult but worthwhile, noting that Zelenskyy has publicly endorsed such a plan. The United States would be willing to help make it happen, Rubio said. Russia's Foreign Ministry made no mention of a partial deal on grain shipments in a statement after the Lavrov-Rubio meeting. The statement reiterated that the root causes of what it calls its "special military operation" must be addressed. At the Security Council, Lavrov said Russia will not "pause" its military action, claiming Europe would use it to "pump" Ukraine with weapons. He also made no mention of any kind of grain and energy deal, called Ukraine's government "terrorists," and Moscow's military operation aims to ensure Russia's security and the rights of Russian speakers. Lavrov is due to address the General Assembly on Saturday. Zelenskyy cast doubt on Russia's interest in ending the fighting. "Something always seems to stop Putin from saying, 'That's it. Enough. Peace,'" Zelenskyy said. "Can you even imagine him without war? He is 'patient zero', the one from whom this idea of war keeps spreading further." "The more freedom Putin has to act, the more dangerous the world becomes for everyone else," the Ukrainian president warned. The war has reverberated across the planet -- with global repercussions for fuel, fertilizer and grain shipments - and for geopolitics, widening divisions between Russia and the West. Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, expecting to take the capital, Kyiv, in a week. But Ukraine rallied to defend its sovereignty, and the conflict has dragged on, with front-line positions in eastern and southern Ukraine largely unchanged since last year. Western analysts estimate that over 500,000 Russian troops have been killed and that Ukraine has recorded more than 500,000 military casualties, including up to 140,000 deaths. Neither country discloses its own casualty totals. Russia and Ukraine have intensified their long-range attacks with drones and missiles, and Russian drones pounded Kyiv Wednesday, killing two people and wounding 23; two others were injured by a strike that started a big fire at a shopping mall in the southern city of Zaporizhzhia. Russia's Defense Ministry said it struck Ukrainian military-industrial and energy facilities, logistics centers, and sea vessels overnight. The ministry said its air defenses intercepted more than 500 Ukrainian drones over multiple Russian regions and Crimea, as well as the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea. Crimea is the peninsula that Russia seized by force and illegally annexed in 2014. Zelenskyy says 'you can stand and survive' Zelenskyy told the assembly that Russia has used 63,000 attack drones of different types against Ukraine so far this year alone. While celebrating that his own country "has proven that even against a much bigger enemy, you can stand and survive," he implored world leaders to deny Putin money or foreign fighters. "Limit his money. Limit his war," the Ukrainian leader said. Zelenskyy said Ukraine must boost its military and has already successfully tested four new jet-powered interceptor drones against Iranian-designed Shahed drones used by Russia in Ukraine. He also heralded drone and anti-ballistic missile agreements and programs with various countries. Zelenskyy worried, however, that artificial intelligence "will begin to decide what happens on the battlefield" with the development of autonomous killer weapons. "We need peace before we reach that point," he said. "Sometimes, it may seem that Ukraine is focused, focused, only on war because we speak about weapons, we speak about defense and sanctions against the aggressor. But Ukrainians did not choose this war," Zelenskyy said. "We choose not to die. .... We are defending ourselves." You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

title: âPlease bring my son backâ: Indian student from Gujarat held in Ukraine after joining Russian Army; cancer-stricken mother seeks help to bring him back
text: Sahil Majothiâs journey from a student in Russia to Ukrainian captivity has left his family desperate for his return. (Photo: The Indian Express) What began as a move to Russia for education has left a 23-year-old student from Gujarat caught in the middle of the Russia-Ukraine war. Sahil Mahmad Husen Majothi, from Morbi, travelled to Russia in January 2024 on a student visa to study Russian language and culture. Within months, he was arrested in a narcotics case and sentenced to seven years in prison. He later signed a contract with the Russian military while in prison and was sent towards the frontline in Ukraine. He eventually surrendered to Ukrainian forces and is now being held in Ukraine, according to the latest report by The Indian Express. His mother, Hasinaben Majothi, has since been fighting to bring her only son back to India. She has approached the Delhi High Court seeking government intervention, while continuing to appeal for help. As per the Independent, she is also undergoing treatment for breast cancer. From Russia for studies to a prison sentence Sahil arrived in St Petersburg on January 10, 2024, on a student visa and enrolled to study Russian Language and Culture at ITMO University. While studying, he also worked part-time as a courier, his family has said. On April 10, 2024, he was arrested in connection with a narcotics case. Sahil's family has maintained that he was wrongly implicated in the case while working as a courier. He was subsequently sentenced to seven years in a Russian prison. The Indian embassy had met him in June 2024 and remained in contact with his family, according to the court proceedings reported by The Indian Express. âI didnât want to stay in prisonâ While in prison, Sahil signed a contract with the Russian military. In a video released after his surrender, he explained that he had joined the Russian forces because he did not want to remain in prison. The Independent reported that Sahil said he had been convicted on drug charges in Russia and had subsequently gone to fight after signing the military contract. Sahil's account of how he ended up in the Russian military has since become an important part of his family's appeal for help. In a later video message, Sahil said he had been âmisled by Russian policeâ and described signing the military contract as the âbiggest mistakeâ of his life, reported The Indian Express. His family has also alleged that he was manipulated and forced into the situation. From the battlefield to Ukrainian captivity Sahil was subsequently sent towards the frontline. He crossed towards Ukrainian positions and surrendered to Ukrainian forces. A video released by the Ukrainian military showed him in custody, identifying himself as an Indian from Gujarat. The Independent had earlier reported in October 2025 that Ukrainian forces had released a video of Sahil after his surrender. At the time, Indian officials were working to verify the authenticity of the video and there had been no formal communication from Ukrainian authorities to New Delhi. In the video, Sahil spoke about his arrest in Russia and his decision to join the Russian military rather than remain in prison. He later sent messages to his family and appealed directly to the Indian government. âRight now I am stuck in Ukraine as a war criminal. Now I am hopeless, I donât know what will happen in future,â he said in one of the messages, according to The Indian Express. He also appealed to Prime Minister Narendra Modi and External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar for help. âPlease take all steps to bring him backâ Sahil's mother subsequently approached the Delhi High Court, seeking government intervention to secure his release and return. During the proceedings, the Centre placed before the court details of Sahil's movements and communication between Indian officials and Russian authorities. The court directed the government to take steps to establish contact with Ukrainian authorities and work towards his repatriation. The court directed that efforts be made to establish contact with the Ukrainian side and that Sahil's family be kept informed. For his mother, Hasinaben, the wait has been particularly difficult. She is undergoing treatment for breast cancer, with her condition currently in remission, while continuing her efforts to secure her son's return. A warning for Indians travelling to Russia In one of his messages from Ukrainian custody, Sahil also addressed Indians considering Russia for education or employment. âThose Indians coming to Russia for higher studies or work, be careful because there are so many scammers here,â he said. Sahil left Gujarat as a student hoping to study in Russia. Within months, he was arrested and sentenced to prison. title: Why Kaliningrad matters to Putin: The SuwaÅki Gap vulnerability, Kremlin's nuclear threat and India link
text: Putin warns of nuclear response over Kaliningrad as the SuwaÅki Gap emerges as a Nato flashpoint. Russian President Vladimir Putin has warned that Moscow could use âall weaponsâ in its arsenal, including nuclear weapons, if its Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad comes under direct attack. The warning has brought renewed attention to a narrow stretch of land between Poland and Lithuania, known as the SuwaÅki Gap, which lies between Kaliningrad and Russiaâs ally Belarus and is considered a potential flashpoint in a conflict between Russia and Nato. Speaking at the Valdai Discussion Club in Moscow on Thursday, Putin said Russia had no plans to attack any European country but would respond if the West escalated tensions or threatened Russian territory. He referred to Nato military activity in the Baltic region, attempts to intercept Russian ships and statements about Kaliningrad. âThe drills in the Baltic Sea, following one another â¦ Then the attempts to arrest our ships and vessels. All this is an escalation. And then we began to hear statements regarding the Kaliningrad region,â Putin said. âIf it comes to direct attack against the Russian Federation, in this case on Kaliningrad and possibly some other territories, of course the issue of using all weapons in our countryâs arsenal will inevitably and unavoidably emerge on the agenda. This is unavoidable,â he cautioned. The remarks followed a Russian diplomatic warning that Moscow could resort to nuclear weapons if Nato attempted to cut off Kaliningrad by land, air or sea. Nato secretary general Mark Rutte said the alliance was defensive and urged Russia to stop its nuclear rhetoric. He also said there was no immediate threat to Nato territory from Russia. Why Kaliningrad matters to Russia Kaliningrad is a heavily militarised Russian territory separated from the countryâs mainland. It is located between Poland and Lithuania, both Nato members, and has a coastline on the Baltic Sea. The region has a population of about one million and is slightly larger than the US state of Connecticut. The territory was formerly known as KÃ¶nigsberg and was the capital of East Prussia. It became part of the Soviet Union after the Red Army captured it in April 1945, towards the end of World War II. The victorious Allied powers subsequently divided East Prussia, and the northern part, including KÃ¶nigsberg, came under Soviet control. The city was later renamed Kaliningrad. Its location gives Moscow a military foothold on the Baltic Sea, far from the Russian mainland but close to several Nato countries. Kaliningrad provides a base for Russian air defence, missile and naval forces, allowing Moscow to project military power into northern and central Europe. That strategic value also creates a vulnerability. Since the region is separated from mainland Russia by the territory of other countries, Moscow would face logistical challenges in supplying or reinforcing it during a conflict. Its land borders are with Poland and Lithuania, while access to the Baltic Sea is subject to the military and political situation in the region. Kaliningradâs position has become more sensitive since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Nato has strengthened its eastern flank, while Finland and Sweden joined the alliance in 2023 and 2024 respectively. Their membership has altered the security environment around the Baltic Sea and added to Moscowâs concerns about the allianceâs military presence in the region. The SuwaÅki Gap vulnerability The SuwaÅki Gap is a narrow stretch of land, around 60 miles long, along the Poland-Lithuania border. It separates Kaliningrad from Belarus, a close Russian ally. It is also the land corridor connecting the Baltic states of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania with the rest of Nato. The SuwaÅki Gap: A narrow corridor at the heart of rising Russia-Nato tensions. The corridor has acquired strategic importance because of what could happen if Russia gained control of it. A Russian military advance through the gap could potentially link Kaliningrad with Belarus and disrupt the land connection between the Baltic states and other Nato members. Also read: What's Suwalki gap? Europe's 'achilles heel' that it fears could be Putin's target Such a move would place Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania in a more isolated position during a conflict. Their security depends on the ability of Nato forces to move personnel, equipment and supplies through Poland and Lithuania. The SuwaÅki Gap is therefore viewed by security analysts as a vulnerable point in the allianceâs eastern defences. The gap is not, however, an established route for an imminent Russian operation. Any attempt to seize it would mean a direct military confrontation with Poland and Lithuania, and therefore with Nato. The possibility is one of the reasons the corridor features prominently in military planning and discussions about the defence of the Baltic states. For Moscow, Kaliningrad is both a military asset and a territory that could become difficult to defend if a conflict disrupted its access routes. For Nato, the SuwaÅki Gap is important because it links the Baltic members of the alliance to the rest of the bloc. This geography makes the region a potential flashpoint, even without an active military confrontation. What has triggered the latest tensions? Tensions around Kaliningrad have increased as Nato has strengthened its presence in the Baltic region following Russiaâs invasion of Ukraine. Moscow has repeatedly criticised Western military activity near the exclave and described comments by European officials about Kaliningrad as threatening. In May 2026, Russia condemned remarks by Lithuaniaâs foreign minister, who said Nato had to demonstrate that it could penetrate what he described as the âsmall fortressâ built by Russia in Kaliningrad and destroy its air defences and missile bases. A Western military source told Reuters that dozens of aircraft from Nato countries took part in an unannounced operation in the airspace around Kaliningrad in mid-August. The operation reportedly demonstrated the allianceâs ability to disrupt the exclaveâs radio and radar links, as well as its air defences, in the event of a conflict. Nato has said its increased presence in the Baltic Sea is partly a response to concerns over threats to critical undersea energy and communications infrastructure. The alliance has also cited the need to strengthen deterrence along its eastern flank. Russia, meanwhile, has accused Nato of escalating tensions and has used diplomatic statements and social media posts by its embassies to draw attention to what it describes as threatening military movements and rhetoric. The alliance has rejected the suggestion that it intends to attack or isolate Kaliningrad. Why a crisis could escalate Analysts have warned that a direct confrontation between Russia and Nato could emerge from a miscalculation rather than a planned attack. Kaliningradâs location makes it particularly sensitive to incidents involving military aircraft, drones, naval vessels or critical infrastructure. Possible triggers include a drone incident, disruption of undersea infrastructure, new missile deployments or an action that Moscow interprets as an attempt to impose a blockade on the exclave. A dispute over access to Kaliningrad could also intensify if military movements in the Baltic Sea or around the SuwaÅki Gap were misread by either side. Since 2022, European countries have supported Ukraine with weapons, intelligence and sanctions against Russia while avoiding direct participation in the war. Moscow has accused Western countries of effectively waging war against it, a charge rejected by Nato members. Putinâs warning over Kaliningrad comes amid this wider confrontation. It does not establish that Russia has decided to use nuclear weapons, but it underlines Moscowâs willingness to invoke its nuclear arsenal in response to what it describes as a direct attack on Russian territory. Nato has said it does not threaten Kaliningrad and has described Russiaâs nuclear warnings as irresponsible. Rutte said the alliance had responded calmly to Moscowâs warning and reiterated its defensive position. Ukraine war adds to pressure on Moscow Putinâs comments on Kaliningrad came as Russiaâs war in Ukraine entered its fifth year. Moscow has continued its offensive and intensified attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure and Kyiv ahead of winter. Ukraine, meanwhile, has stepped up drone strikes on Russian oil refineries and other targets deep inside Russian territory. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has described such strikes as âlong-range sanctionsâ, aimed at reducing Russiaâs revenue and military capacity and pushing the Kremlin towards negotiations. Putin acknowledged that Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries had affected the countryâs economy. He said the strikes had cost Russia about 1% of its gross domestic product. He also said Ukrainian military operations in the Black Sea had damaged or destroyed more than 100 Russian ships. âIn the Black Sea â thatâs a combat zone; we struck military vessels and ships transporting military cargo, and we hardly ever made a mistake. Throughout this whole saga, they [Ukraine] have knocked out over 100 of our ships. Well, we started hitting back, and now weâre being bombarded from every direction with appeals: âOh, please stop doing that,â Putin said. âItâs the same story with our oil refineries; they (Ukraine) openly declared their goal was to damage our economy. Did they succeed? Partially â by our estimates, we lost about one percent of our GDP. And it was done deliberately â these are civilian targets, after all. Well, they got a mirror-image response,â Putin added. His remarks came a day after he told newly elected members of Russiaâs State Duma that the countryâs economy was stable. He also criticised Ukraineâs reliance on financial assistance from Western allies, saying Russia did not need external handouts. âMistakes, especially now, are absolutely unacceptable,â he warned parliamentarians. âUnlike some, and we wonât point fingers, Russia canât run around the world humiliating (itself) by begging for handouts with an outstretched hand,â he said. Putin has said he would prefer the war to end through negotiations, but has not indicated that Moscow is prepared to withdraw from its military objectives. A Levada Center poll in August found that 59% of Russians favoured moving towards peace talks. Russiaâs planned defence spending also points to a continued military commitment. Budget documents reviewed by Reuters show that Moscow plans to spend 17.1 trillion roubles ($205.112 billion) on defence in 2027, about 27% more than originally budgeted and the highest level since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. India's military connection to Kaliningrad Beyond its strategic importance in European security, Kaliningrad has a direct defence connection with India through the Russian Yantar Shipyard. Located in the exclave, Yantar has built several warships for the Indian Navy, including two upgraded Talwar-class frigates, INS Tushil and INS Tamal. Both vessels were constructed in Russia and commissioned into the Indian Navy at Kaliningrad. INS Tushil was launched at Yantar Shipyard on October 28, 2021, and commissioned in December 2024. INS Tamal, the second frigate under the project, was commissioned at the same facility on July 1, 2025. The two vessels are part of a four-frigate arrangement between India and Russia under Project 1135.6. The agreement involves constructing two ships in Russia and two in India, with technology transfer and design assistance from the Russian side. The commissioning of INS Tamal marked the completion of the Russian-built portion of the project. However, India's naval cooperation with Russia has not ended with the delivery of these two warships. The remaining two frigates, INS Triput and INS Tavasya, are being constructed at Goa Shipyard Limited (GSL) in India. The first vessel, Triput, was launched on July 23, 2024, while Tavasya was launched on March 22, 2025. Both are based on the Project 1135.6 design and are intended to undertake surface, sub-surface and air combat operations. The ships are 124.8 metres long, have a displacement of approximately 3,600 tonnes and can achieve a maximum speed of 28 knots. Their construction represents India's transition from directly procuring warships from Russia to manufacturing them domestically with foreign design assistance. The ministry of defence has described the project as part of India's efforts to strengthen indigenous warship construction. The vessels incorporate a large percentage of Indian-origin equipment, weapons and sensors. These include localised components such as the BrahMos missile system, torpedo launchers, sonar and auxiliary control systems. Is India still dependent on Kaliningrad? India is no longer receiving complete frigates from Kaliningrad under this particular project. title: 'He made a mistake but can't admit it': Russia's ex-PM says Putin 'not ready' to end Ukraine war
text: Putin not ready to negotiate Ukraine war end despite âmistakeâ, says Russiaâs ex-PM Russian president Vladimir Putin is not ready to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine despite growing economic pressures and unease among sections of Russian society and the elite, former prime minister Mikhail Kasyanov said on Saturday. Kasyanov, who served as Russiaâs prime minister from 2000 to 2004, said Putin understood that invading Ukraine in 2022 had been a mistake but remained unwilling to change course. Watch Putin Ready For âNATO WARâ: 600+ Drones POUR FIRE, Robot Army UNLEASHED In Massive Military Show âHe made a mistake that he cannot bring himself to admit,â Kasyanov, 68, told AFP in Paris. âHe believed the reports from his security services that Ukraine was weak.â Kasyanov said he was not convinced the war would end next year, arguing that high oil prices linked to the US-Iran conflict and disagreements between the United States and Europe over dealing with Moscow had strengthened Putinâs position. âPutin is, of course, rubbing his hands with glee,â he said. âHe clearly believes he can continue the war without making any concessions. And he is convinced that he is winning a war of attrition against Ukraine.â The former prime minister warned that the coming winter could be particularly difficult for Ukraine and urged Western countries to apply âpsychological pressure on the Kremlinâ by maintaining unity and urgently supplying Kyiv with Patriot missile interceptors. Putin, a former KGB officer who turns 74 on Wednesday, has repeatedly said millions of Russians support the war. His ruling party won a record supermajority in elections last month, a result critics said followed a tightly controlled process. Kasyanov, who left Russia in 2022 and now lives in exile in Riga, said he remained in contact with members of the Russian ruling elite. âFear reigns there -- I am talking about the ruling class,â he was quoted saying. âEveryone wants the war to end. An overwhelming majority does", he told AFP. He said views differed over how the conflict should conclude, with some seeking victory, others wanting Putinâs defeat and some simply wanting the fighting to stop. Among ordinary Russians, Kasyanov said he saw âno grounds for a revoltâ despite casualties and rising food prices. âRussians have lived with high inflation for the past 30 years,â he said. âThey have grown accustomed to putting up with it.â However, he warned that another large-scale mobilisation could trigger street protests. Kasyanov, who joined the opposition after being dismissed by Putin, described Russia as âpractically totalitarianâ and said there was âa sense of fatalism, hostility toward one another, and serious tension in societyâ. On Putinâs recent warning that Russia could use âall types of weaponsâ if Kaliningrad were attacked, Kasyanov urged Western countries not to be intimidated. âThe West's and Europeans' biggest mistake is that they are too afraid of Putin. He is not as strong as he appears,â he said. âPutin fears the nuclear button more than many Europeans do.â Kasyanov said he did not believe Putin was preparing for open war with Europe, arguing that Moscowâs objective was to force European countries to acknowledge Russia. âWhat Putin wants is respect. title: Russia to take 70,000 Indian skilled workers this year, Jaishankar tells panel
text: EAM S Jaishankar poses for a group photo with other dignitaries after a consultative committee meeting on India-Russia relations NEW DELHI: External affairs minister S Jaishankar on Saturday briefed a parliamentary consultative committee on India's "multifaceted" engagement with Russia, covering bilateral trade, investment and energy cooperation as well as New Delhi's diplomatic efforts to contribute towards ending the Ukraine conflict. Chairing the meeting on India-Russia relations, Jaishankar also informed members that Russia has agreed to take around 70,000 Indian skilled workers this year, particularly in construction and logistics, people familiar with the discussions said, according to news agency PTI. Watch âIf Concludedâ: Jaishankarâs BIG Trade Deal Message To U.S, As Essar Bets $18-Bn On Trumpâs America Jaishankar said India and Russia share an ambition to expand bilateral trade in a more balanced manner, including by increasing Indian exports to Russia across seven sectors â automobiles, pharmaceuticals, food, marine products, engineering goods, chemicals and textiles. The discussions also covered an India-Eurasian Economic Union Free Trade Agreement, the Chennai-Vladivostok corridor, the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC) and the Northern Sea Route. On energy cooperation, Jaishankar said India's priority was to safeguard the interests of Indian consumers. "Our approach is to maintain multiple sources of supply," he said, according to people familiar with the meeting. The government has also been seeking to expand opportunities for Indian workers in Russia. The minister referred to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's August 31 meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Bishkek, where the PM said that "endless war must now give way to end of war". title: Russia cuts welfare, education and healthcare budget as war spending hits new high
text: The government is also spending more on servicing its debt as high interest rates increase borrowing costs. Russia is preparing to cut spending on welfare, education and healthcare in its 2027 federal budget while raising taxes, as the government struggles to meet the rising cost of its war in Ukraine, according to fiscal documents reviewed by Reuters. The draft budget proposes 17.1 trillion roubles ($202.58 billion) for defence in 2027. That is about 27% higher than the 13.5 trillion roubles originally allocated for defence and would be the highest military spending level since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Military spending takes priority The increase in defence spending comes as Russia's finances have come under growing pressure during the four-and-a-half-year war. Moscow has used its fiscal reserves, borrowed more money and raised taxes to help finance its expanding military expenditure. The new budget would reduce spending on social policy by 7% from the initial plan. This area covers state pensions, payments to war veterans and maternity benefits. Education spending would fall by 6%, while healthcare funding would be cut by 6.8%. Spending under the "national economy" category, which includes road building, infrastructure projects and subsidies for agriculture and other industries, would also fall by 7.4%. Russia is preparing a three-year budget to improve long-term financial planning, but its budget projections have repeatedly been revised as the war has continued. The government has also missed its annual deficit targets several times. Higher taxes and rising household costs The pressure on public finances is also being felt through higher taxes and other costs. The 2027 draft budget includes new tax increases, while utility tariffs are also expected to rise by more than previously planned. Those measures have angered some supporters of the Kremlin, particularly after they were announced following this month's parliamentary election. The new State Duma is expected to approve the budget. The pro-Kremlin United Russia party is set to retain a constitutional majority, while Russian authorities have repeatedly said that winning the war in Ukraine takes priority over other spending needs. Debt costs add to the pressure Russia's financial burden is not limited to military spending. The government is also spending more on servicing its debt as high interest rates increase borrowing costs. Debt-servicing costs in 2027 are expected to be 21.6% higher than originally planned. They are projected to account for 9.4% of total government spending next year and could rise further to 10.6% by 2029. The federal budget does not include regional and municipal spending, which also accounts for a significant portion of Russia's social expenditure. Even so, the latest figures show how the prolonged war is forcing Moscow to devote more of its finances to defence while putting pressure on other areas of government spending. You use AI every day. title: South Korea accuses Ukraine of breaching secrecy over North Korean POW transfer
text: South Korea says Ukraine broke confidentiality over North Korean POW transfer South Koreaâs presidential office has sought an official explanation and apology from Ukraine over the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea. Seoul accused Kyiv of disclosing the transfer and then falsely denying that the two countries had agreed to keep the move confidential. South Korean President Lee Jae Myung had earlier said Ukraine breached a non-disclosure agreement by disclosing the transfer. In a post on X, Lee said âit was appropriate in every aspect not to discloseâ the transfer, citing its potential consequences, and said the two sides had agreed to keep the matter confidential. âI do not know what circumstances led the Ukrainian side to disclose the matter despite the confidentiality agreement, but it is deeply regrettable,â he wrote. âThe presidential office expresses strong regret over Ukraineâs unilateral disclosure and its subsequent false announcement that there had not been a non-disclosure agreement,â Seong Ghi-hong, senior presidential secretary for public relations, said in a statement released on Sunday. Seong said the South Korean government was reviewing additional measures over the issue, if necessary. He said Ukraine had repeatedly discussed the transfer of the prisoners with Seoul through various channels and had requested that the matter be kept confidential. According to Seong, Kyiv feared that publicly disclosing the transfer could trigger domestic criticism that it had given up an opportunity to exchange the North Korean soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners. Seong said South Korea had agreed to keep the transfer confidential due to security, diplomatic and humanitarian concerns, including the safety of the prisoners and their families. However, according to the statement, Ukraine later disclosed the transfer during President Volodymyr Zelenskyyâs address to the United Nations General Assembly without sufficient prior consultation and subsequently denied that any confidentiality agreement had been reached. Seong said Ukraineâs denial had seriously damaged trust between the two governments and could affect bilateral relations. Ukraine captured the two North Korean soldiers in Russiaâs Kursk region in January 2025. They were the first North Korean soldiers to be captured alive after Pyongyang entered the war in 2024 in support of Russia, as cited by Reuters. South Korea had earlier declined to confirm their arrival, citing concerns over the safety of the soldiers and their family members in North Korea. Seoul and Kyiv had been discussing a possible transfer after the two soldiers expressed a desire to travel to South Korea, according to an opposition lawmaker in Seoul. The transfer comes as South Korea has supported efforts to revive dialogue with North Korea, while US President Donald Trump has renewed his willingness to engage with Pyongyang. title: Zelenskyy, after meeting Trump, says Ukraine ready for 'energy ceasefire' with Russia
text: Zelenskyy stressed that he had not agreed to unilaterally stop Ukrainian attacks on Russia's oil industry. Ukraine is ready to halt attacks on Russian energy facilities if Moscow agrees to stop striking Ukraine's power and other critical energy infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said after meeting US President Donald Trump in New York. Zelenskyy said the proposal for an "energy ceasefire" was discussed as the two leaders held a 40-minute meeting on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly. He also warned that Ukrainian intelligence had detected preparations for what he described as a major new Russian attack. Writing on X, Zelenskyy called his meeting with Trump "positive and productive" and said both countries wanted to end the war before winter. "Both the US and Ukraine want to see this senseless Russian war ended before winter. We discussed potential de-escalatory steps that can open up the way to diplomacy," he added. Kyiv offers reciprocal energy truce Speaking to reporters at the UN headquarters, Zelenskyy said Ukraine was prepared to stop hitting Russian energy targets, but only if Russia stopped its own attacks on Ukraine's energy network. "We are ready for energy ceasefire," he said. "If they donât want us to attack their diesel and refineries, and etc, we are ready â if they will not attack our energy system, our electricity, heating system, water supplies." Zelenskyy stressed that he had not agreed to unilaterally stop Ukrainian attacks on Russia's oil industry. Trump had raised the issue of Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries before meeting Zelenskyy. The US president said the attacks had damaged Russian fuel-processing capacity and were also affecting diesel prices. "It is a serious hit on the Russians. Itâs also a serious hit on the price of diesel," Trump said. Trump said the two leaders would also discuss ways to end the war, which began with Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. "I think itâs going to happen," he added. Previous energy deal failed to hold Trump said last week that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop attacking each other's energy infrastructure. However, attacks resumed soon afterwards. Moscow had previously backed a US proposal for an energy moratorium, while also seeking measures covering Russian seaborne energy exports and sanctions. Zelenskyy, however, rejected any immediate discussion about easing sanctions against Russia while Ukrainian cities remained under attack. Following a meeting with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, he wrote on Telegram that there could be no discussion of sanctions relief "when Ukrainians live every day under the threat of missile and drone attacks". He added that Ukrainian intelligence had detected preparations for another major Russian offensive. "Thereâs intelligence right now that Russia is preparing a new â massive attack against Ukraine," he wrote. Russia and Ukraine intensify energy strikes The latest proposal comes after weeks of attacks by both sides on energy infrastructure and other strategic targets. Russia has repeatedly struck Ukrainian power, fuel and port facilities. Kyiv has also been preparing for further attacks on its energy network as winter approaches. On September 15, Ukrainian officials said Russia launched about 200 drones across the country. The attacks hit petrol stations in Kyiv as well as energy and port infrastructure in other areas. Ukraine has meanwhile stepped up its long-range drone campaign against Russia's oil industry. Its strikes have targeted refineries and other energy facilities as far as 3,000km from the Ukrainian border. A September 20 strike reportedly forced the Moscow oil refinery to stop crude processing. The refinery processed around 230,000 barrels of crude oil a day in 2024, according to industry sources cited by Reuters. title: Seoul summons Ukraine envoy, demands apology after Zelenskyy reveals North Korean POW transfer
text: Zelenskiy told the UN General Assembly last week that Ukraine had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to South Korea. Seoul called for an official apology from Ukraine after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy revealed, what it says was a secret transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea. Zelenskyy revealed to the UN General Assembly last week that the soldiers were captured on a battlefield between Russia and Ukraine in early 2025, and that Ukraine had delivered them to South Korea. Thousands of North Korean soldiers, including the two, have been dispatched to aid Russia in its conflict with Ukraine. Lee Jae Myung, the president of South Korea, immediately accused Ukraine of breaking a nondisclosure agreement over the transfer. Ukraine denies entering into such an agreement. Seong Ghi-hong, Lee's senior presidential public relations advisor, voiced "strong regret" at Ukraine's recent actions late on Sunday and called for an official apology and justification. Andrii Vieshkin, the ambassador of Ukraine to Seoul, was summoned by the South Korean Foreign Ministry on Monday to protest what it called Kyiv's "unilateral disclosure" of the inmates' transfer, and its false denial that the two nations had agreed to keep the matter quiet. According to a statement from the ministry, Vieshkin promised to communicate Seoul's stance to his administration. The Ukrainian Embassy in Seoul did not respond to repeated demands for comment. Seong said that Ukraineâs âfalseâ denial of the nondisclosure agreement was âan act that seriously undermines trust between the two governments and causes significant damage to friendly relations between the two countries.â According to Seong, the arrangement was achieved because Kyiv was afraid about potential political backlash for losing the chance to trade them for Ukrainian troops detained in Russia, while Seoul was anxious about the safety of the North Korean soldiers, and their families in the North. POWs from North Korea desired to relocate to South Korea. The two troops stated in interviews with the media that they intended to relocate to South Korea while they were still in Ukraine. Seoul has urged Ukraine to refrain from returning them to North Korea, where they may be persecuted. The South has a policy of welcoming and providing financial help to North Korean defectors, and it officially views the North as part of its territory. Since the end of the 1950â53 Korean war, over 34,000 North Koreans have escaped to South Korea, primarily in the previous three decades. The majority were female citizens from the impoverished northern regions of the North. Soldiers seldom defect. Zelenskyy stated in his statement to the United Nations that "one of them attempted suicide, when he knew he was going to be captured", and was taken aback by that. He was spared death by fate. In the North, individuals are raised in this manner. According to some observers, Zelenskyy probably chose to highlight the threat posed by North Korea's involvement in the conflict in order to secure greater support from the West. The liberal administration of South Korea, meantime, was concerned that the transfer's announcement may incite a furious reaction from the North, and undermine attempts to restore diplomatic relations between Washington and Pyongyang. South Korea has declined to provide Ukraine with direct military assistance. Since Russia's invasion in 2022, South Korea, a rising arms exporter with a well-equipped, and US-backed military, has joined US-led economic sanctions against Russia, and given humanitarian supplies and other support to Ukraine. However, in keeping with a long-standing policy of not delivering weapons to nations actively involved in combat, Seoul has rejected pleas from Kyiv and NATO to offer direct military help to Ukraine. In April 2025, North Korea and Russia acknowledged that their armed forces had engaged in joint combat to thwart a Ukrainian invasion of Russia's Kursk border area. According to South Korea, the US, and others, North Korea has also given Russia missiles, artillery, and ammunition in exchange for military and economic support. According to South Korea's spy agency, 2,000 of the approximately 15,000 personnel that North Korea supplied were killed last year. Kim Jong Un, the leader of North Korea, has been able to more assertively pursue a nuclear weapons development, and resist pressure from the United States by increasing collaboration with Russia. In an apparent attempt to resume diplomatic relations with Kim, US President Donald Trump reduced a military exercise with South Korea this month. However, North Korea has stated that this action was insufficient to persuade it to resume negotiations. In protest of Kyiv's revelation of the transfer of arrested North Korean troops to South Korea, South Korea's foreign ministry called Ukraine's acting ambassador on Monday, and requested an official apology and explanation. Despite what Seoul claimed was a clear agreement between the two nations to keep the matter confidential, the ministry said it had called in acting ambassador Andrii Vieshkin, and expressed deep regret that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy made the disclosure at the UN General Assembly. According to a statement from the ministry, South Korea also objected over what it deemed a misleading statement made by the Ukrainian presidential office denying the existence of such a confidentiality agreement, and asked Kyiv to take action to stop a repeat. "First Vice Minister Park Yoon-joo stressed that the disclosure of a falsehood that there was no confidential agreement seriously undermines trust between the two governments and is an action that can cause problems for friendly ties," added. He said the aim was to disrupt daily life and pressure people to leave Kyiv and other cities. âWe have to respond in any way we can. With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refiners etc: what gives money to them for this war,â Zelenskyy said. He said Ukraine would respond against Russian energy infrastructure but would not deliberately target civilian facilities. From energy grids to bridges The shift comes as Russian attacks on Kyiv have increasingly focused on infrastructure that keeps the capital functioning. Over the past week, Russian drones and missiles have struck energy and telecommunications assets as well as road and rail infrastructure. Russia has also targeted bridges over the Dnipro River connecting eastern and western Kyiv, marking a new pressure point on the city's transport network. The attacks point to a broader form of infrastructure-based warfare in which the objective is not only to destroy military positions, but to disrupt the systems that allow a city to function: electricity, communications, transport, logistics and supply routes. Moscow says its strikes are retaliatory responses to Ukrainian attacks on Russian territory. Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilians. Zelenskyy, however, said Ukrainian intelligence documents showed the Russian objective was to make life in Ukrainian cities increasingly difficult. âThey allow them to attack infrastructure, logistics, and especially to attack in the cities, in the villages, everywhere, roads, schools, hospitals,â he told Reuters. âTo pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities: this is the goal of the operation.â Ukraineâs answer: hit what funds Russiaâs war Zelenskyy said Ukraine's response would focus on Russian energy infrastructure, particularly oil refineries that generate revenue for Moscow's war effort. Zelenskyy said he had seen no indication that Moscow was ready to resume meaningful negotiations or agree to a ceasefire covering energy infrastructure. Ukrainian officials say Russia has stockpiled hundreds of ballistic missiles ahead of a new campaign. Last winter, Russian strikes repeatedly damaged energy infrastructure, leaving parts of the country without electricity and heating for extended periods. Russia has also expanded its use of faster jet-powered Shahed drones, which Ukrainian air defences have struggled to intercept. Zelenskyy said Ukraine was relying heavily on F-16 and MiG fighter aircraft to destroy them, but ammunition supplies for the aircraft were running low. Kyiv is therefore working on cheaper alternatives, including electronic jamming and new interceptor drones. Zelenskyy said two models had been tested but were achieving a success rate of only around 30% so far. The infrastructure campaign is unfolding alongside fighting over territory in eastern Ukraine. title: Europe has learned to negotiate security in Greenland. Why can it not do the same in Ukraine?
text: . Europe has reached a decisive moment in its modern history. The conflict in Ukraine has evolved into a broader crisis of European security, strategic autonomy, economic resilience and political judgement. Defence spending is rising, energy security has been disrupted, public finances are under pressure, and relations between Russia and the West have deteriorated dramatically. Yet beneath the increasingly militarised language of European governments lies a fundamental question: what political settlement can ultimately bring the conflict to an end? The answer cannot be found exclusively on the battlefield. Military power can alter the balance of forces, but it cannot, by itself, create the political conditions for lasting peace. A sustainable settlement requires an understanding of geography, sovereignty, national security and the interests of Ukraine, Russia, Europe and the United States. Diplomacy is not the opposite of security; it is one of its essential instruments. The agreement signed by Denmark, Greenland and the United States on 22 September 2026 provides a striking example. The agreement respects the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark and Greenlandâs right to self-determination, while strengthening US military access and NATO engagement in the Arctic. It allows the United States to modernise and expand activities at Pituffik Space Base and establish additional defence areas at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig. That is precisely what makes Greenland relevant to Ukraine. If Denmark and Greenland can negotiate a security arrangement that takes account of American, Danish, Greenlandic and NATO interests, why should Europe not be capable of imagining a comparable diplomatic architecture for Ukraine? Ukraine could remain permanently neutral. It would not join NATO, and there would be no permanent NATO or Russian military presence on its territory. At the same time, Ukraine would remain sovereign, maintain its own armed forces and political system, trade with the European Union, maintain relations with the United States, and preserve diplomatic and economic relations with Russia and the wider world. Its security could be protected through credible international guarantees. Such an arrangement would not mean surrendering Ukraine to Russia. It would mean refusing to turn Ukraine into a permanent military frontier between rival blocs. The political significance of this debate becomes clearer when we examine developments within Europe itself. European governments increasingly speak about rearmament, military preparedness and long-term confrontation. Millions of Europeans, however, are confronting higher living costs, expensive energy, pressure on household finances and growing concerns about public services. Every additional military commitment also carries an opportunity cost. Money devoted to prolonged confrontation cannot simultaneously be devoted to hospitals, schools, transport, housing and welfare. Germany provides a particularly striking example. In the September 2026 election in Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD won 43.8 percent of the vote and 39 of 83 seats, while the CDU received 17.2 percent and 15 seats. On 20 September, the AfD again came first in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania with 38.2 percent and 32 of 71 seats, ahead of the SPD with 35.5 percent. The CDU received 4.9 percent and failed to enter the state parliament. In Berlin on the same day, Die Linke came first with 25.7 percent, followed by the CDU with 18.8 percent and the AfD with 16.3 percent. These results do not establish why every individual voted as they did, but they demonstrate substantial dissatisfaction with Germanyâs established political direction. The AfD has campaigned against continued military support for Ukraine and in favour of a different relationship with Russia. The results have also increased political pressure on Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who described the Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania result as a âdisasterâ while stating that he would remain chancellor. France provides another indication of political change. Marine Le Penâs Rassemblement National remains a major political force. Across Europe, there is growing political demand for negotiations, greater attention to national interests and an end to permanent escalation. The point is not that every voter in these parties shares the same foreign-policy position. Rather, European governments should not assume that citizens will indefinitely accept confrontation as the only viable policy. Europe should also pay attention to voices advocating diplomacy. Slovakiaâs Robert Fico has opposed further military assistance to Ukraine and direct involvement. Italyâs Matteo Salvini has repeatedly called for negotiations. Austriaâs neutrality provides another example of a European state maintaining a security policy outside military alignment. The danger of escalation is not theoretical. On 14 September, a Danish military helicopter was conducting a routine photographic operation near a Russian frigate in international waters off Denmark when the Russian vessel fired two flares towards the aircraft. According to the Danish Armed Forces, one passed at close range, while Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus said it came within a matter of metres. Russia, for its part, accused the Danish helicopter of dangerous manoeuvres. The incident illustrates how quickly routine military surveillance can develop into a potentially dangerous confrontation between NATO and Russian forces. This is precisely why a peaceful diplomatic end to the conflict in Ukraine is essential. Europe should not allow a chain of military encounters, miscalculations and escalating responses to create circumstances in which a local incident develops into a direct confrontation between major military powers. Europe should not allow the Ukraine conflict to become a pathway towards a third world war. Its political leaders have a responsibility to create diplomatic space before military logic closes it. This is also where Donald Trumpâs approach deserves attention. Trump has repeatedly made ending the war and restoring US-Russia relations explicit objectives. His emphasis on direct engagement with Moscow reflects an important diplomatic principle: even profound disagreements between major powers must ultimately be addressed through negotiation if a durable settlement is to be achieved. Whatever disagreements may exist over Trumpâs broader policies, his pursuit of peace negotiations deserves recognition. Russia cannot simply be removed from the European security equation. Any settlement must address Ukrainian sovereignty and security while also engaging with the security concerns that Russia says underpin its position. India offers another useful example. New Delhi has demonstrated that it is possible to maintain strategic relations with both Russia and the United States. Indiaâs longstanding partnership with Russia continues alongside a substantial relationship with Washington. This is strategic autonomy: constructive relations with one major power do not require hostility towards another. Europe could apply the same principle to Ukraine. A sovereign Ukraine can maintain strong economic relations with Europe, close relations with the United States and normal diplomatic relations with Russia without becoming a military outpost of any one bloc. The Greenland agreement demonstrates that security arrangements can be negotiated around competing strategic interests. Ukraine needs its own negotiated security architecture, one that protects its sovereignty while reducing military confrontation between Russia and NATO. If Europe has learned to negotiate security in Greenland, it should be able to negotiate security in Ukraine as well. Disclaimer : Views expressed above are the author's own.

title: Switzerland's neutrality test puts Nato ties, Russia sanctions at stake
text: An electoral poster reads âNo war, Yes to Swiss neutralityâ is posted along a road in Epagny, Switzerland (AP) Swiss voters are deciding on Sunday whether to tighten the country's neutrality rules, in a referendum that could restrict its peacetime military cooperation with Nato and limit its ability to impose sanctions on countries involved in wars. According to Reuters, the proposed constitutional amendment would prevent Switzerland from cooperating with military or defence alliances during peacetime, unless the country itself were attacked or an attack were imminent. It would also restrict Switzerland from joining sanctions against countries involved in conflicts, with exceptions including measures mandated by the United Nations. Switzerland is not a Nato member, but it has maintained cooperation with the alliance for decades while retaining its neutral status. Nato says Switzerland joined the Partnership for Peace programme in 1996 and cooperates with the alliance on areas including military interoperability, defence capabilities and peace-support activities. The proposed changes could therefore affect existing forms of Swiss-Nato cooperation. Reuters reported that Swiss foreign minister Ignazio Cassis has warned that the initiative could prevent Switzerland from training with Nato and reduce its ability to prepare for potential security crises. Russia sanctions at the centre of debate The referendum also puts Switzerland's policy towards Russia under scrutiny. Bern adopted sanctions against Moscow following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, largely aligning itself with measures imposed by the European Union. Supporters of the initiative, led by the right-wing Swiss People's Party, argue that such measures have compromised Switzerland's neutrality. Christoph Blocher, a prominent backer of the proposal, told Reuters that Russia now considers Switzerland a party to the conflict because of its sanctions. The initiative would establish a stricter framework under which Switzerland could generally not participate in sanctions unless they were imposed by the United Nations or fell under specified exceptions. Government warns against isolation The Swiss government opposes the proposal, arguing that neutrality does not mean isolation. Bern says Switzerland can remain neutral while cooperating with other countries to strengthen its security. The government has also argued that military cooperation and interoperability need to be developed during peacetime rather than only after a conflict begins. The debate has gained significance as European countries strengthen their defence capabilities amid the continuing Russia-Ukraine war. The referendum is therefore not about whether Switzerland will remain neutral. Instead, it is about how strictly that neutrality should be applied and whether it should limit Switzerland's military and diplomatic cooperation with other European countries. You use AI every day. title: Putin warns West of 'all weapons' use if Russiaâs exclave Kaliningrad is attacked
text: Putin acknowledges that Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries were hurting the countryâs economy Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday warned the West against escalating the war in Ukraine, saying Russia could use âall weaponsâ in its arsenal, including nuclear weapons, if its Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad comes under attack. Speaking at the Valdai Discussion Club in Moscow, Putin said Russia had no plans to attack any European country but would respond if it faced what he described as Western aggression. He specifically pointed to Kaliningrad, a Russian territory located between Nato members Poland and Lithuania. âIf it comes to direct attack against the Russian Federation, in this case on Kaliningrad and possibly some other territories, of course the issue of using all weapons in our countryâs arsenal will inevitably and unavoidably emerge on the agenda. This is unavoidable,â Putin said. âThe drills in the Baltic Sea, following one another â¦ Then the attempts to arrest our ships and vessels. All this is an escalation. And then we began to hear statements regarding the Kaliningrad region,â Putin said. Putin says Ukraine strikes hitting Russian economy Putin also acknowledged that Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries were hurting the countryâs economy, saying they had cost Russia about 1% of its GDP, CNN reported. Ukraine has stepped up long-range drone attacks on Russian territory, particularly targeting oil infrastructure. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has described the strikes as âlong-range sanctionsâ intended to cut Russiaâs revenues and military capacity and push Moscow towards negotiations. Putin said Ukrainian attacks had also damaged more than 100 Russian ships in the Black Sea. Why is Kaliningrad strategically important? Kaliningrad is a strategically important Russian territory surrounded by Nato members Poland and Lithuania. It is a heavily militarised Russian exclave, meaning it is separated from Russiaâs main territory. Located between Poland and Lithuania on the Baltic Sea, the region has a population of about 1 million and covers an area slightly larger than the US state of Connecticut, Reuters reports. The exclave gives Russia a key military position in the Baltic region, hosting air defence, missile and naval capabilities that can project power into parts of northern and central Europe. But its location also makes it vulnerable. Surrounded by Nato territory on its landward sides and separated from mainland Russia, maintaining supply lines or reinforcing the region could become difficult during a conflict.
