title: US to lend 40 million barrel oil from strategic reserve as Ukraine war strains global supply
text: The move comes amid an energy crisis that has erupted due to the escalating Russia-Ukraine war, and Americaâs inconclusive conflict with Iran (Photo: Reuters). United States on Tuesday offered to loan energy companies 40 million barrels of oil from its Strategic Petroleum Reserve, an attempt to control rising prices due to the Ukraine and Iran conflict. In March, the United States committed to lend 172 million barrels of oil from the SPR, forming part of a broader agreement among roughly 30 International Energy Agency member countries to release 400 million barrels in total. In June, the Trump administration offered to lend the final 40 million barrels under that IEA arrangement. Later that month, however, it disclosed that companies had agreed to borrow only around 500,000 barrels. The move comes amid an energy crisis that has erupted due to the escalating Russia-Ukraine war, and Americaâs inconclusive conflict with Iran. Ukraine has been increasingly targeting Russian energy facilities in order to curb the financial resources that sustain Russian war efforts. On Sunday night, it struck oil facilities in Russiaâs Krasnodar region. "We are consistently using our long-range capabilities to respond to Russian strikes", Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on X, adding that Moscow must stop escalating the conflict. Oil strain on India Meanwhile, Reuters reported on Tuesday that Indian refiners expect Russian oil supplies to decline further in October and November. Lower Russian exports and fierce competition from China are forcing the country to buy costlier alternatives for the rest of the year. "Demand from China has been really high. They were willing to book cargoes in advance and to pay firmer prices compared to Indian refiners," said a source involved in the sale of Russian crude. Analytics firm Kpler expects Russian oil arrivals in India to fall to about 1.75 million barrels per day in September, the lowest level since April. Trade data showed that arrivals had already dropped 16.5 per cent from July to around 2.1 million bpd in August, though Russia remained India's main supplier, ahead of the UAE and Venezuela. The overall availability of Russian exports has reportedly shrunk, especially from the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk, where shipments have roughly halved because repeated drone attacks have suspended loadings. title: AI sings Russia's war story: Inside the rise of generative songs about Ukraine conflict
text: Among the songs whose release dates could be established, most appeared after 2024. (Reuters photo) Artificial intelligence is being used to produce a growing number of songs about the Russia-Ukraine war, with some of the music presenting Russia's invasion in a favourable light and criticising Ukraine. Hundreds of such tracks have appeared on major music streaming platforms, including Spotify, Apple Music, YouTube and Deezer, according to research by Terrecon, a Ukrainian nonprofit organisation focused on threat intelligence. The songs cover a wide range of musical styles, from ballads to heavy metal. Terrecon said some praise Russian soldiers, describe the war from a Russian perspective and contain derogatory references to Ukrainians, including ethnic slurs. One of the more popular tracks identified by the organisation is âPower of Artilleryâ, a Russian-language rock song centred on artillery systems including Krasnopol and Carnation. Nearly 1,000 songs identified Terrecon said it catalogued 981 songs created with AI that contained what it classified as pro-Russian war propaganda. Among the songs whose release dates could be established, most appeared after 2024. That coincided with the wider availability of AI music generators such as Sudo and Udio. The technology has lowered the time and cost involved in producing music, according to Daria Verbytska, a founder of Terrecon. âThey have found new ways to create cheaper drones and use them on a massive scale,â Daria Verbytska, a founder of Terrecon, said told NYT in a telephone interview, referring to the Russians. âItâs like that with music â creating massive propaganda with the help of AIâ Some of the songs use themes associated with Soviet-era war music but present them through contemporary genres. One track, âSoldier's Daughterâ, describes the death of a soldier and the impact on his child while also portraying the soldier's sacrifice in a positive light. It is not clear how much involvement, if any, the Russian government has had in producing or distributing the songs. However, the Kremlin has supported cultural projects aimed at promoting patriotic themes. Last week, a director of Moscow's Internet Development Institute, an organisation that works closely with the Kremlin to promote patriotic values, said in a presentation that the institute had supported more than 350 artistic projects related to the war, according to Russian media reports. AI tools can produce war-related music Terrecon also tested several AI music generators to see how they responded to prompts requesting songs promoting Russian views of the war. Researchers used Suno, Udio and Google Flow Music in the US, along with Singapore-based Mureka. They entered prompts in both Russian and English, including requests involving violence and derogatory descriptions. The platforms rejected some prompts, but researchers said they were nevertheless able to generate songs resembling some of those in Terrecon's database. They then uploaded the tracks to YouTube Music and SoundCloud. âThe moderation systems mainly responded to specific banned words rather than the overall meaning of the prompts,â Terreconâs report found. The researchers said the issue is partly linked to the differing rules adopted by AI music services and streaming platforms. They also said automated systems may have difficulty identifying expressions, slang and offensive language in different languages. Streaming platforms tighten AI rules Major music platforms generally have policies covering hate speech and violent content, although fewer have specific rules dealing with propaganda. Deezer and YouTube are among the platforms that require certain AI-generated content to be labelled. Spotify said in September that it had introduced a policy to label AI-generated songs and prevent them from being recommended to users. The company also added labels to songs shared by The New York Times as examples. Terrecon said the songs it identified had been played millions of times across major streaming services, although the extent to which listeners understood that some of the music was AI-generated or politically motivated is unclear. Deezer spokesman Jesper Wendel said the platform reviews potentially rule-breaking content on a case-by-case basis. SoundCloud spokeswoman Sade Ayodele said the company reviews reported content and added that âthere is no place on SoundCloud for content that incites or glorifies violence.â The emergence of these songs illustrates how AI music tools can be used to produce and distribute large volumes of war-related material. It also presents streaming and AI companies with the challenge of deciding how existing rules on hate speech, violence, political content and AI-generated material should apply to such music. title: Russia targets Ukraine's digital nerve centres as war reaches data infrastructure
text: Four people were killed in a Russian drone strike on a business centre in Kyiv, Ukrainian officials said Russia is expanding its strikes on Ukraine's critical infrastructure to include data centres and telecommunications facilities, disrupting internet services for around 100,000 households in Kyiv and the surrounding region. According to the BBC, citing Ukrainian officials, Russian strikes damaged data centres operated by internet providers in Kyiv. On Friday, a Russian drone hit the Inkom business centre in the capital, which housed a Datagroup data centre, killing four people and damaging the facility. Datagroup said its services continued to operate from backup sites. Kyiv Data Hub Under Fire: Did Russia Just Strike At Ukraine's STARLINK Lifeline? Watch Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia had widened its attacks to target Ukraine's data centres and internet providers, seeking to cause maximum disruption to ordinary people. "All this affects people's ability to stay connected, study, work," Zelenskyy said, arguing that the attacks were increasingly affecting essential aspects of daily life. Russia, however, said it had targeted the data centre because it was being used by Ukrainian military intelligence. The Russian defence ministry confirmed the strike on the Datagroup facility and said its forces had also targeted other data-processing and telecommunications centres in Ukraine, including New-Telco, United DC, Kyivstar and Parkovyi. The attacks come alongside continued Russian strikes on Ukraine's energy and railway infrastructure, widening the focus of the war to the digital systems that support civilian life and essential services. Importance of data centres for military operations Data and computing infrastructure have become increasingly important to modern military operations. Center for Strategic and International Studies said modern military operations are increasingly dependent on data and require large amounts of computing power, rapid access to information and the ability to integrate data across systems. CSIS said Ukraine is fighting a data-driven, AI-enabled war in which the strategic migration of data to cloud locations inside and outside the country has helped maintain its operational resilience. CSIS has also documented how Ukraine's military uses digital systems to collect, process and analyse battlefield information. Its Delta situational-awareness system, gathers data from multiple sources and processes it through cloud infrastructure to provide commanders with a real-time operational picture, supporting battlefield decision-making and command and control. CSIS reported that Ukraine moved significant parts of its digital infrastructure to public cloud systems and data centres outside the country, helping it maintain government and digital services despite Russian cyber and physical attacks.

title: US-Russia talks on Ukraine now involve multi-billion dollar oil deal tied to Trump & his allies
text: Lukoil oil deal enters US-Russia-Ukraine talks Talks between the US and Russia over ending the war in Ukraine have expanded to include a proposed multibillion-dollar deal for Lukoilâs international oil assets, with the prospective investor group including people with business ties to US President Donald Trumpâs allies. The deal would require approval from both the US government and the Kremlin. The proposed transaction covers Lukoilâs overseas portfolio of oil fields, refineries and gas stations. A group led by US investor Todd Boehly has emerged as the leading bidder, alongside Middle Eastern investors and the US government. The details were reported by The New York Times, citing eight people familiar with the negotiations. The negotiations have also brought renewed attention to the business links of Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who are leading US efforts to engage Moscow on the Ukraine war. There is no indication that Witkoff or Kushner would personally profit from the proposed transaction. However, the deal has raised questions about the overlap between the Trump administrationâs diplomatic efforts with Russia and the business interests of people connected to the president and his allies. Putin raised Lukoil deal with US negotiators Russian President Vladimir Putin raised the proposed Lukoil transaction when he met Witkoff and Kushner at the Kremlin on September 5, according to people familiar with the meeting. Putin reportedly presented the deal as a potential way to demonstrate that Russian and US businesses could resume working together. The US side indicated it would work on the proposal, viewing it as a possible means of building goodwill with Moscow while potentially helping lower global energy prices. The proposed sale would also benefit buyers because US approval could release the assets from American sanctions, increasing their value. Lukoilâs international holdings include oil fields in Cameroon, refineries in Europe and gas stations in the US. While Lukoil is technically a private company, the decision over the deal is seen in Moscow as one that ultimately depends on Putin. Who is seeking Lukoilâs assets Boehly, co-owner of the Los Angeles Dodgers, is leading the group currently seeking the assets. He donated $1 million to MAGA Inc. in December 2025 and another $1 million through his investment firm to Trumpâs inauguration. The proposed investor group also includes Qatar-based businessmen Moutaz and Ramez Al-Khayyat and an Abu Dhabi investment fund controlled by Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan. The Al-Khayyat brothers have business ties with Kushner and his wife, Ivanka Trump, including a planned luxury resort project in Albania. Sheikh Tahnoon controls an investment fund that acquired a significant stake in World Liberty Financial, the Trump family-linked cryptocurrency company co-founded by Witkoff. Trumpâs sons are also involved in the company. Witkoff has since sold his stake, according to a person close to him. Sheikh Tahnoon also oversees Lunate, an Abu Dhabi investment fund that is among the major stakeholders in the private equity firm founded by Kushner after he left the White House. US approval remains crucial The Lukoil deal is not final and requires approval from the US treasury department, which oversees sanctions enforcement. The Trump administration had sanctioned Lukoil in October 2025 as part of measures targeting Russiaâs energy sector and pressing Moscow over the Ukraine war. A senior US administration official said, as quoted by NYT, Witkoff and Kushner had directly participated in negotiating the financial terms of the proposed US government investment, including âa substantial upfront payment and profits interest for the United States.â Previous Lukoil bid stalled The Lukoil assets have attracted several potential buyers since the company put its international holdings on the market. US private equity firm Carlyle reached a tentative agreement in January to acquire a large portion of the assets, but US approval for that bid stalled. The Boehly-led group subsequently emerged as the leading bidder. The treasury department has had to repeatedly extend sanctions-related arrangements while the sale remains unresolved. The latest extension is due to run until October 29. Lukoil valued its international assets at about $20 billion earlier this year, although the price and structure of the proposed transaction have not been disclosed. The proposed sale comes as the Trump administration seeks to use the prospect of renewed economic ties with Russia as part of its broader effort to persuade Moscow to compromise over Ukraine. Witkoff and Kushner have repeatedly travelled to Russia for talks with Putin as Washington pursues an end to the war. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

title: Airlines wake up to âinsider threatâ after flydubai attack
text: Airlines wake up to âinsider threatâ after flydubai attack NEW DELHI: The unprecedented incident aboard flydubaiâs Dubai-Tel Aviv flight has added a ânew dimensionâ to aviation security, prompting calls for airlines to conduct regular psychometric evaluations of pilots amid concerns about an âinsider threatâ. Airlines with a significant proportion of expatriate crew, particularly in the Gulf, may also need to be more careful when rostering pilots of different nationalities on specific routes. Israel vets crew of all flights landing in the country. Going by that, there was talk that the flydubai co-pilot â an Omani national, according to Israel foreign minister Gideon Saâar â ought not to have been rostered on this flight. Saâar has termed the incident a âjihadist terror attackâ, adding that though thereâs no evidence yet, the main motive was to derail Israel-UAE ties. âAirlines conduct psychometric evaluation at induction and then mostly at the time of command upgrade (when a co-pilot becomes a captain) and other promotions, such as that to be a trainer,â said a senior official of an Indian airline. âIn big airlines with a large number of crew members, frequent pairing of the same set of personnel does not happen. So, even if someoneâs conduct is amiss, no one is likely to notice, and this leads to poor peer-to-peer reporting. There has to be greater surveillance for this issue now. Unlike weapons and explosives hidden in baggage that can be detected, it is difficult to fathom what is going on in a personâs mind.â Union aviation secretary Samir Sinha called the flydubai incident âunfortunateâ, adding, âBut we are very proud of Captain Smit. We would not like to delve into it as it pertains to some other country. The matter is under examination, and an internal deliberation is on to decide whether any security advisory is needed to be issued.â Airlines in nearby regions â particularly the Gulf, but also Southeast Asia and Sri Lanka â employ many Indian pilots who are not rostered on flights to Pakistan. A senior Indian pilot working for a foreign airline recalled flying to Karachi about two decades ago, when his aircraft developed a snag. âI was the only one who did not get a crew visa to leave the airport, and had to sleep in the aircraft. The next morning, I was sent on a flight to Dubai by my airline,â he said. Israel conducts background checks on foreign crew members scheduled to operate flights to the country before allowing them entry. Another Indian pilot, who works for the general aviation arm of a large foreign airline, said: âAs a rule, Indian passport-holders are not assigned charters to Pakistan. When the Russia-Ukraine war erupted, European pilots were not sent to Russia flights. Aircraft were not allowed to fly direct from Venezuela to the US and we used to travel via some third country. That changed when Venezuelaâs then president Nicolas Maduro was captured this Jan. â Geopolitical tensions have worsened since Covid, with the Russia-Ukraine and India-Pakistan conflicts and the US-Iran war turning the regionâs skies into a virtual minefield. Western airlines do not overfly Russia. When an Air India flight between India and North America diverts to Russia, US passport-holders breathe easier once they board an alternative aircraft to their destination. Diversions to Pakistan also cause unease among passengers on flights to or from India. âThe global situation must cool down fast, as it is deepening the fault lines of the region,â said an official. title: âMobilizing mythâ: Why is Russia sending dead princes, saints into Ukraine battle
text: Russian soldiers stand guard during military operations in the region Russian troops fighting in eastern Ukraine are receiving an unusual form of support as the war enters another winter. Relics of medieval Russian rulers and warrior saints are being taken to military bases and units at the front. In early September, a fragment of the remains of Dmitry Donskoy, the Moscow prince celebrated for his victory at the 1380 Battle of Kulikovo, was sent to Russian troops and is now being moved around military bases in Russian-occupied Ukraine. The relic is a fragment of his right hand, the same hand the Russian Orthodox Church says he used to wield his sword in battle. Watch Trump-Zelensky Meet Sparks Moscow Claim; Kyiv Denies Putin Meeting Proposal? The military department of the Moscow Patriarchate said the âsaint commanderâ would invisibly stand âshoulder to shoulderâ with Russian soldiers. The move is part of a broader role the Russian Orthodox Church has played during the war, with religious symbolism being used alongside state narratives about Russiaâs military campaign, according to a CNN report. âThe church has practically merged with the state to the point of being indistinguishable,â the report quoted Sergei Chapnin saying, a religious scholar and director of communications at Fordham Universityâs Orthodox Christian Studies Center. âFrom my point of view, the maximum (closeness) has been reached.â Why Donskoyâs relics were taken to the front The practice of taking sacred relics to troops is not new in Orthodox Christianity. But experts say Donskoyâs medieval military legacy gives the relic a particular significance in the context of the Ukraine war. Chapnin said Donskoy is presented not as an aggressor but as a defender of his homeland, allowing the historical figure to be linked to Russiaâs present-day narrative about the war. âHe was not himself an aggressor, but a defender of the fatherland,â the scholar told CNN. From the governmentâs perspective, âit is very important to show that Russia is not the aggressor, that we are defending our territory.â Chapnin described this connection between Russiaâs medieval past and its current war as âa mobilizing myth.â âThese myths, which connect different times and eras, can act quite powerfully on mass consciousness,â he said, adding that the relics are presented as âa magical artifact.â Metropolitan Vladimir, the Russian-installed Orthodox leader in Donetsk and Mariupol, said the relic would help soldiers and civilians âmobilize both their spiritual and physical strengthâ and âtriumph over the enemy.â Donskoy is not the only medieval Russian ruler whose relics have been taken to the war zone. Earlier this year, relics of Prince Alexander Nevsky, another ruler later turned into a symbol of Russian military glory, were also taken to troops. From Kremlin to Church, a closer wartime relationship The use of religious relics comes against the backdrop of a closer relationship between the Kremlin and the Russian Orthodox Church since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The Church has repeatedly used religious language to support Russiaâs military narrative. The recovery of Donskoyâs remains in August was itself given religious and historical significance by Russiaâs political and religious leadership. President Vladimir Putin called the recovery an âabsolutely uniqueâ and âmarvelous discoveryâ, while Patriarch Kirill described it as âa special sign of Godâs providence.â The relics have also been displayed in Moscow, where thousands participated in religious events involving Donskoyâs remains. An annual religious procession in September drew more than 100,000 people in Moscow alone, according to official figures. But the role of the Church in the war has drawn criticism from within the wider Orthodox community. For Rev Alexander Zanemonets, an Orthodox priest and historian, the use of Donskoyâs remains âhas nothing to do with Christianity.â âIt is undoubtedly the exploitation of Christianity and the exploitation of the church for âpatrioticâ purposes," CNN quoted him saying. He argued that the Churchâs strong state backing creates incentives to align with the Kremlin, calling the use of the remains a âcynical calculation.â What soldiers make of it The religious symbolism does not necessarily have the same meaning for troops at the front. Some Russian soldiers say faith has become more important as the war continues. A former Russian serviceman told CNN that soldiers often turn to God during difficult moments. âNot all of us talk to God when things are going well, but everyone talks to God when things are bad,â he said. He described makeshift churches at the front, soldiers praying before missions and priests visiting military units and hospitals. âLike a field kitchen, there should be a priest everywhere,â he said, quoting a popular Russian expression: âWe are Russians. God is with us.â A Russian soldier serving in the Zaporizhzhia region described being able to speak to a priest, pray or touch a holy object as âserious moral support.â But not all soldiers see the relics as meaningful. One serviceman in the Donbas region called the decision to send them to the front âa very unconventional solution to our problems in the 21st century.â âMy view is that they are needed more by the mothers of the guys who died in this military operation,â he added. The war has also raised questions within the Orthodox community over the role priests should play in supporting soldiers. Rev Grigory Mikhnov-Vaytenko, a Russian priest who helps Ukrainian refugees displaced by the war, said spiritual support should not become a means of reinforcing an illusion about the conflict. âWe need to support people, including those in military uniform,â he said. âBut the question is how we support them.â âOn the one hand, (you must) not deny people spiritual help, and on the other, not lead them into an illusion,â CNN quoted the priest as saying. The debate comes as the war enters its fifth year, with Russian soldiers describing mounting strain at the front. For the Kremlin and the Russian Orthodox Church, however, the medieval warrior saints and their relics offer a way to connect Russiaâs military present with its religious and historical past. title: âPeople of Russia support our effortsâ: Putin says record turnout shows Russians back his military agenda in Ukraine
text: File photo: Russian President Vladimir Putin (Picture credit: AP) Russian President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday said high voter turnout in the country's parliamentary election showed public support for his policies and for the armed forces fighting in Ukraine, after preliminary results gave his United Russia party a record parliamentary majority. More than 97% of the votes had been counted, with United Russia expected to win more than three-fourths of the 450 seats in the State Duma, according to election officials cited by news agency AP. Near-complete results showed the party securing 355 seats, or nearly 80% of the lower house, after winning more than 57% of the vote. The election, held over three days from September 18 to 20, was the first parliamentary poll since Putin launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. It was also the first to include residents of four Ukrainian regions that Russia seized and declared annexed later that year. Ukraine has rejected the voting in those territories as illegal. Putin links turnout to support for war effort Putin, speaking publicly about the results for the first time, said turnout demonstrated support for the government's policies. âSuch a high, even record, number of people who came out and voted shows that the people of Russia support our efforts aimed at strengthening the country,â he said, according to Reuters. Russia's Central Electoral Commission put turnout at 59.3%, while AP reported that turnout exceeded 59% of the 111 million eligible voters, making it the highest for a parliamentary election in more than a decade. Putin also directly addressed Russian troops fighting in Ukraine. âThis vote is for you. People believe in you, believe in our victory, believe in your courage, in your heroism,â he said. Putin further said, âI have no doubt that all the goals we set for the special military operation will be fulfilled,â using the Kremlin's term for the war. Voting held amid Ukrainian drone attacks The election took place amid continued Ukrainian drone attacks on Russia. Russia's defence ministry said it had shot down 1,110 drones overnight on Sunday. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 450 drones targeting the capital were downed in what he described as the city's âlargest everâ attack. Officials said the attacks damaged an oil refinery and a residential building and killed three people and injured 38 in the wider Moscow region. âThey tried to hamper our efforts, to derail the election, as evidenced by the enemyâs continuous efforts to breach air defenses around Moscow and in other regions,â Putin said. âBut lines at polling stations have shown that Russia canât be intimidated.â Authorities extended voting to three days and used online voting in some regions. Voting was also held in Crimea, which Russia annexed in 2014, and in the four Ukrainian regions claimed by Moscow. United Russia set for record majority Preliminary results indicated that United Russia would win between 347 and 355 seats. The party secured just under 58% of the party-list vote for 225 seats and won 208 single-seat constituencies, which make up the other half of the Duma. Several smaller parties that form Russia's âsystemic oppositionâ are expected to take most of the remaining seats. Only a small number are expected to go to candidates who ran without party affiliation. The liberal Yabloko party, which had publicly criticised the war, was removed from the ballot by Russia's Supreme Court last month and had only a limited number of candidates in single-seat contests. Preliminary results showed that none of its candidates had won a seat. The election was conducted under extensive state media coverage and tight political controls, while voting also took place in territories whose annexation by Russia has been rejected by Ukraine. title: Russia escalates Ukraine infrastructure attacks, strikes second Kyiv bridge in days
text: File photo: A Russian jet powered drone strikes on one of Kyiv's bridges, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Kyiv, Ukraine Russia struck a second major bridge in Kyiv within days on Saturday, damaging the road surface and trolleybus cables and forcing the suspension of traffic across the Dnipro, as Moscow stepped up attacks on critical infrastructure in the Ukrainian capital. The Northern Bridge was hit during a Russian air attack, Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko said. Emergency services were deployed to the scene, while traffic from the east bank to the west bank was blocked. No casualties were reported. The strike came after Russia repeatedly targeted Kyivâs Southern Bridge with drones on Thursday and Friday, disrupting one of the capitalâs key transport links. The attacks on the two bridges mark a new phase in the latest Russian campaign against Kyivâs infrastructure. The bridges connect the eastern and western sides of the city, whose roughly 3 million residents depend heavily on the transport network to cross the Dnipro. Kyivâs bridges come under repeated attack The Southern Bridge was struck several times over the previous two days, forcing authorities to temporarily suspend traffic across it as well as two other bridges over the Dnipro. The attacks caused major disruption for commuters. More than a third of Kyivâs residents lived on the eastern, or âleftâ, bank of the river before Russiaâs 2022 invasion, while most government institutions and companies are located on the western, or ârightâ, bank. Klitschko had earlier warned that the attacks were putting Kyiv in a âvery dramatic situationâ as Russian strikes hit the cityâs critical infrastructure, logistics and housing. After one strike on the Southern Bridge, passengers described how the blast wave sent dust through the ventilation system of a train carriage. The latest attacks have revived memories of last winter, when Russia launched some of the warâs most damaging strikes against infrastructure supplying Kyiv with power. The attacks came after Russia launched what Ukraine viewed as the opening salvo of an expected winter campaign targeting energy facilities serving the capital. Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia was seeking to destroy not only bridges but also data centres, internet and mobile networks, hospitals, schools and other civilian infrastructure in an effort to force people to leave Ukrainian cities. Russia has previously denied systematically targeting civilians during its bombing campaigns. Russian president Vladimir Putin has said Moscowâs attacks are a response to Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure. title: Another Donald Trump-Putin meeting soon? US invites Russian President to G20 summit in December
text: US invites Putin to G20 amid fresh diplomatic push over Ukraine war US secretary of state Marco Rubio has said Russian President Vladimir Putin has been invited to the G20 summit in the United States in December, describing the gathering as an opportunity for him to engage with US President Donald Trump and other world leaders. Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, Rubio said the Trump administration remained open to engaging with leaders with whom it disagreed, arguing that direct meetings could help address difficult issues. âSo we've invited President Putin to the G20. We think it's an opportunity for him to engage not just with the President (Trump), but with other world leaders. We hope that's an invitation he'll accept, that there's an opportunity in December if that happens,â Rubio said. Rubio's remarks came after he met Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, with the two discussing the Russia-Ukraine war and US-Russia bilateral relations, according to the US State Department. Rubio says Trump open to meeting Putin Explaining Trump's approach to diplomacy, Rubio said the US president was willing to meet people even when there were disagreements between them. âPresident (Trump) is willing to engage and meet with virtually anyone,â Rubio said, adding that Trump believed that âin order to solve problems, you have to meet with the people that you disagree with or the people that you might have some issues with.â Rubio said a meeting between Trump and Putin would ideally have a clear purpose and result, requiring substantial preparation beforehand. âObviously, the ideal would be a meeting in which there will be a result, an outcome. And a lot of that means there has to be a lot of work that goes into it beforehand,â he said. He added that Putin's possible attendance at the G20 could provide an opportunity for the two leaders to interact. âBut if not, maybe if President Putin attends the G20 in December, that will certainly be an opportunity for them to interact and talk,â Rubio said. Rubio also said Trump and Putin had spoken on the phone numerous times since Trump took office, estimating that they had held at least a dozen conversations. Russia-Ukraine ceasefire proposals discussed The G20 invitation comes as Washington continues to engage with Moscow and Kyiv over the Russia-Ukraine war. Rubio said on Wednesday that both Russia and Ukraine had expressed interest in a limited ceasefire covering grain and energy, according to Reuters. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has also said Ukraine was ready for a maritime truce in the Black Sea based on proposals from Egypt, India and Turkey. He said Ukraine was waiting for Russia's response and was prepared to work towards safe shipping and food security if Moscow was ready to take steps towards de-escalation. âWe are waiting for Russia's response. Ukraine is ready ... to ensure safe shipping and food security in the Black Sea if Russia is ready to take real steps towards de-escalation too. We have to start somewhere,â Zelenskyy said. Zelenskyy also said he was ready to meet Putin in a trilateral meeting with Trump. The Kremlin, however, has said there are currently no prerequisites for broader Ukraine peace talks, while maintaining that Russia remains open to negotiations. âFor now, there are no prerequisites for moving on to a peaceful negotiating track, although we, as the Russian side, remain open to peace talks,â Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said. The latest diplomatic contacts come as the US continues discussions with both sides on possible limited ceasefires involving energy infrastructure and grain, alongside broader efforts to address the Russia-Ukraine conflict. title: âFatal point of no returnâ: Putin warns against use of nukes amid global tensions
text: Russian President Vladimir Putin attends Valdai International Discussion Club in Moscow (Picture credit: Reuters) Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday warned that the world was living through a dangerous moment, saying escalating international conflicts could reach a âfatal point of no returnâ and stressing that weapons of mass destruction must never be used. Speaking at the Valdai Forum of international Russia experts in Moscow, Putin said the worldâs leading powers possessed arsenals capable of destroying all life or reducing the Earth to a âcatastrophic stateâ. He urged countries to recognise how quickly escalating retaliation could lead to an irreversible situation. âWe must realise that the moment when nothing can be changed any longer may come very quickly and unexpectedly for everyone. The logic of escalating, increasingly harsh retaliatory measures leads to a fatal point of no return,â Putin said. âAt the heart of this escalation lie arrogance and overconfidence. This is a path to the brink of the abyss. All the more so today, when the arsenals of the worldâs leading powers contain weapons capable of destroying all life or, at the very least, reducing the Earth to a catastrophic state. Can we be certain that these weapons will never be used? Well, of course not. We must bear this in mind and avoid such an outcome.â Putin warns of Western role in Ukraine conflict Putin said Ukraine would not be able to carry out attacks deep inside Russia without Western technical support, arguing that such assistance amounted to direct involvement in the conflict. He said Russia viewed attempts to use Ukraine as a proxy to fight Russia as a threat. Putin also said Moscow was not planning to attack factories in other countries that manufacture weapons for Ukraine, but warned that Russia's military and intelligence services needed to closely monitor them. âWe are not going to attack tomorrow enterprises in countries which supply weapons to Ukraine, but that's a threat,â Putin said. Putin also said Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries had cost Russia 1% of its gross domestic product. He said Ukraine had âpartially achieved its objectivesâ through the attacks, but added that Russia was responding in kind. He further said Ukraine had damaged more than 100 Russian vessels in the Black Sea and that Moscow was now responding. Russia issues warning over Kaliningrad Putin said Russia would consider using the full range of weapons in its arsenal if its Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad came under threat. He maintained that Russia did not plan to attack anyone but would respond to aggression. âWe are not going to attack anyone, but will respond if we face aggression,â Putin said. Kaliningrad is a Russian territory on the Baltic Sea separated from mainland Russia by other countries and located between Nato members Poland and Lithuania. The region has become a focus of tensions between Moscow and the alliance. In a separate development on Thursday, the Kremlin said Russia's recent letter to Nato on Kaliningrad should not be viewed as confrontational. The document accused the alliance of pursuing a âdangerous and reckless courseâ carrying âhigh risks of the outbreak of a direct armed conflictâ. Putin also said Russia was not threatening European countries and did not plan to attack them. âWe are not threatening anyone and we do not plan to attack any European countries, not in 2030, not in 2050,â he said. Putin says global conflicts likely to continue Putin said international conflicts were likely to continue as the global order undergoes fundamental changes, although he said the situation would improve as what he described as Western hegemony waned. âRegardless of which scenario unfolds globally in the coming years, the continuation of international conflicts is, unfortunately, highly likely. This is due in part to the fact that ongoing fundamental shiftsâand the opportunities they presentâfuel ambitions and a willingness to take risks for the sake of a seemingly massive payoff,â Putin said. He again stressed the need to avoid catastrophic scenarios. Putin also said Russia supported a possible trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump, although he said an agenda for such talks would first need to be worked out. On the Middle East, Putin said he hoped the Strait of Hormuz would remain open to shipping and that sanctions on Iran would be lifted. He also said Russia's proposals to deliver enriched uranium from Iran to Russia remained valid. Putin said Russia remained interested in cooperation with Japan but was concerned about what he described as the country's militarisation. He added that Japanese companies continued to operate in Russia and that Moscow supported them and others working with Russia. He also criticised military drills and arrests of Russian vessels as forms of escalation and said Russia had a competitive advantage in defending itself. You use AI every day. title: Russia elections: Putin ally Ramzan Kadyrov wins Chechnya polls with nearly 100% vote
text: The election is the first parliamentary vote since full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. (Reuters photo) Russia's ruling United Russia party, which supports President Vladimir Putin, has won the country's State Duma elections, while his close ally, Ramzan Kadyrov, has been re-elected in Chechnya region with nearly 100 per cent of the vote. Kadyrov been re-elected for a fifth term as the leader of the muslim majority region, securing 99.85 per cent of the votes, while Putin's party secured 355 of the 450 seats overall. The three-day parliamentary election ended on Sunday, with the final results expected by September 25, according to CNN. Early figures released by Russia's Central Election Commission showed United Russia well ahead of other parties. The election is the first parliamentary vote since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Putin has sought to present the poll as a measure of public support for his government's domestic and military policies. Putin links vote to support for troops Ahead of the election, Putin urged Russians to turn out and portrayed the poll as a show of unity behind the country's military campaign. âYour choice and determination will show once again that millions of people are backing our fighters and that we stand together, united by shared values, our historical memory, love for our Motherland,â Putin said, according to CNN. Putin himself was not a candidate in the election. He is due to face voters in the next presidential election in 2030. United Russia won 343 of the 450 seats in the State Duma in the previous parliamentary election in 2021. Opposition largely absent The election took place in a tightly controlled political environment, with CNN reporting that meaningful opposition to the Kremlin was largely absent. Yabloko, the country's only registered anti-war party, was prevented from contesting the federal party-list election after Russia's Supreme Court barred it last month. Overall voter turnout stood at 56.66 per cent, according to the Central Election Commission, while participation in Moscow was also reported to be high. With the result largely expected amid the lack of credible opposition, turnout and the final distribution of the 450 seats are being closely watched. Ukraine war overshadows voting The parliamentary election coincided with intensified military activity between Russia and Ukraine. CNN reported that Ukraine launched more than 1,000 drones towards Moscow and the surrounding region on Sunday. Russian officials said at least two people were killed and a major oil refinery was damaged. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said the attacks were intended to disrupt the election. Ukraine has not independently confirmed that claim. The Kremlin is expected to use the election result to demonstrate domestic support for Putin and his policies, including the war in Ukraine. title: People jump from building windows to escape as Russian jet-powered drone hits Kyiv science academy - video
text: Russia deploys jet-powered drones in fresh wave of strikes, hits Ukraineâs science academy in Kyiv Kyiv academy hit as Ukraine reports surge in Russian jet-powered drone attacks (Video credit: X/MFAUkraine) Russia deploys jet-powered drones in fresh wave of strikes, hits Ukraineâs science academy in Kyiv Kyiv academy hit as Ukraine reports surge in Russian jet-powered drone attacks (Video credit: X/MFAUkraine) Russia deploys jet-powered drones in fresh wave of strikes, hits Ukraineâs science academy in Kyiv 1 2 A Russian jet-powered drone struck Ukraineâs National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv, prompting a rescue operation, Ukraineâs foreign ministry said. Videos circulating on social media appeared to show people jumping from the buildingâs windows as they tried to escape the strike. The incident came amid a wider wave of Russian attacks across Ukraine that killed three people and injured at least nine in Kyiv, according to Ukrainian officials. The extent of the damage to the academy building and the number of people affected were not immediately clear. The foreign ministry said the academy, one of Ukraineâs central scientific research institutions, had been hit in the heart of Kyiv. It called on UNESCO to support the countryâs scientific community and strip Russia of its voice and voting rights within the organisation. "The National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine is one of our countryâs central institutions of scientific research, bringing together generations of Ukrainian researchers. Today, its building in the heart of Kyiv was hit by a Russian strike. A rescue operation is ongoing. Russia continues to strike civilian sites across Ukraine, damaging essential infrastructure. Every Russian strike must receive a strong response and increased pressure on the aggressor. We call on @UNESCO to stand with Ukraine's scientific community and strip Russia of its voice and voting rights within the organisation." Three killed in Russian attacks across Ukraine Russian attacks killed three people in two Ukrainian cities on Sunday, while strikes on Kyiv injured nine people, including a child, local officials said. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said six of the injured were being treated in hospital. A drone struck a high-rise apartment building in an eastern suburb, triggering a fire that was later extinguished by emergency crews. Drones also hit areas near a kindergarten and a playground in two districts, while debris from another drone caused a fire elsewhere in the city. No casualties were reported in those incidents. In the northern city of Sumy, three glide bombs struck near a family support centre, killing two people, regional governor Oleh Hryhorov said. In Kharkiv, a drone hit a car, killing the driver, prosecutors said. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy condemned the attacks, describing strikes on civilian targets as "terrorism". "Russia has no military objective whatsoever in doing this," Zelenskiy wrote in a post on X. "It is purely an attempt to break people and inflict as much harm as possible on our society." Zelenskyy said Russia had deployed 277 attack drones of various types since Saturday, including 155 jet-powered drones. He also said targets in Kyiv included a building used as a residence by the Saudi Arabian ambassador. Ukraine reports attacks on communications infrastructure Ukraineâs largest mobile service provider told Interfax Ukraine that Russian forces had struck its headquarters amid continued attacks on the countryâs data centres and communications infrastructure. There were no casualties, the company said. Russiaâs defence ministry said its forces had struck two data centres, according to Reuters. The ministry did not provide further details in the material available. Why jet-powered drones are harder to intercept Russiaâs use of jet-powered drones marks a further development in its long-range aerial attacks on Ukraine. Earlier models, including the propeller-driven Geran-1 and Geran-2, were slower and could be easier for air defences to intercept. A report published by The Conversation said Russia had introduced successive jet-powered variants, including the Geran-3 in 2025 and the Geran-4 later that year. The Geran-5 was first used operationally in August 2026, according to the report. The Geran-5 has a reported top speed of about 600 kilometres per hour, a range of up to 1,000 kilometres and an operating altitude of around 6,000 metres. title: Iran, Russia and now Ukraine: Why ballistic missiles are reshaping modern war
text: Ukraine fired the FP-7 short-range ballistic missile at a Russian target, this is the first use of such a weapon by Ukraine. (Image credit: Fire Point) Ukraine says it has used its domestically developed FP-7 tactical ballistic missile in combat for the first time, marking another milestone in the country's rapidly expanding indigenous long-range strike programme. The war ravaged country's president Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced the combat debut, adding that the large scale production of the weapon would follow, though the claim remains unverified, with Ukrainian military hasn't disclosed the target, location or number of missiles involved. According to Fire Point, the manufacturer of the ballistic weapon, the FP-7 has a range of around 250 kilometres, carries a warhead of about 150 kg, and travels at roughly 1,500 metres per second, translating to over 5,400 km an hour. Rather than striking deep inside Russian territory, it is designed for closer targets such as logistics hubs, air defence sites and drone bases, making it a shorter-range complement to the American-supplied ATACMS rather than a replacement, albeit one that comes without restrictions on what it can target. Fire Point, a Ukrainian firm that began with drones before expanding rapidly into long-range cruise and ballistic missile technology since Russia's invasion. Ballistic missiles are becoming central to modern warfare. Iran's extensive missile attacks have repeatedly demonstrated the value of these systems, striking targets hundreds of kilometres away without exposing pilots to enemy air defences. During the ongoing confrontation, Tehran fired large numbers of ballistic missiles, several of which penetrated Israeli and allied defences, their speed and steep terminal trajectory leaving defenders only a narrow window to detect and intercept them. These tactical ballistic missiles, along with drones and cruise missiles, force an adversary to juggle multiple types of interceptors simultaneously. Russia has leaned on the same logic throughout its war on Ukraine, deploying systems like the Iskander-M and Kinzhal alongside cruise missiles and drones against military and energy infrastructure, compressing the window Ukrainian air defence commanders have to respond. That pressure is precisely why Kyiv has pushed to build its own tactical ballistic missile capability, reducing reliance on Western-supplied systems while building a layered domestic strike architecture of its own. India has pursued a parallel path with its indigenous Pralay missile, cleared for induction in 2022, with roughly 120 units approved and further Army procurement reportedly in the pipeline. Developed by DRDO, the solid-propellant, quasi-ballistic missile has a range of 150 to 500 km depending on configuration. This weapon uses a manoeuvrable re-entry vehicle to complicate interception, and underwent back-to-back range-validation trials in July 2025. Its conventional warhead gives India a rapid-reaction tactical strike option against command centres, air defence systems and radar installations, without drawing every strike into the country's nuclear deterrence framework. The wider neighbourhood is moving in the same direction. Pakistan continues expanding its Shaheen and Nasr systems, reportedly with Chinese assistance on solid-fuel rocket motor technology, while China's build-up dwarfs both, with an extensive mobile missile force, expanding silo infrastructure, and an estimated 620 nuclear warheads as of 2026, growing faster than any other nuclear-armed state, according to Sweden based Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI).

title: UN report finds widespread sexual violence in Ukraine war, 89% of cases linked to Russia
text: File photo: Smoke rises following a Russian missile attack in Kyiv, Ukraine (AP Photo) Russian forces committed widespread sexual violence against civilians and prisoners of war in Ukraine, including gang rape, genital mutilation and electric shocks to the genitals, while Ukrainian authorities were also responsible for a smaller number of violations, according to a UN human rights report released on Friday. The report by the UN human rights office documented 1,004 verified cases of conflict-related sexual violence between February 2022, when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and July 2026. Of these cases, 89% were attributed to the Russian side, including members of its armed forces, prison service and security agencies, while 11% were linked to Ukrainian authorities, including members of the Ukrainian armed forces, according to Reuters. Russia's permanent diplomatic mission in Geneva declined to comment on the report. Russian forces accused of abuse in detention The report said Russian authorities committed sexual violence against Ukrainian prisoners of war and civilian detainees in occupied areas of Ukraine and inside Russia at various stages of captivity, including during capture, transfer, interrogation and detention. The documented violations included gang rape, rape, genital mutilation and electric shocks to men's genitals using a Soviet-era field telephone known as a âtapikâ. The findings were based on interviews with victims of sexual violence committed by both sides. The UN cautioned that the figures were not comprehensive because conflict-related sexual violence remains significantly under-reported. The report also said Russia's refusal to give the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights access to occupied Ukrainian territory, prisoners of war and civilian detainees meant the actual scale of violations was likely higher. Most victims in detention were men, particularly prisoners of war and detainees, although women and children were also affected, mainly in Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine. âSexual violence in conflict is often misunderstood to be mainly affecting women and girls, where in the Ukraine war context, the majority of survivors are men,â Danielle Bell, head of the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine, said. âAnd men and women require different solutions and approaches to their recovery,â she added. Ukraine also accused of violations The report documented a smaller number of cases involving Ukrainian authorities. In Ukrainian government-controlled territory, nearly half of the violations attributed to Ukrainian authorities against Russian and third-country prisoners of war and detainees involved threats of sexual violence and beatings to the genitals. OHCHR said it did not document any cases of rape of Russian prisoners of war by Ukrainian forces. Russian and third-country prisoners of war reported sexual violence in 10 official detention facilities and 55 unofficial or transit locations, the report said. Ukraine's foreign ministry welcomed the report, saying it demonstrated the scale of human rights violations perpetrated by Russia as well as measures being taken by Kyiv to prevent such violence and compensate victims. The ministry did not directly address the findings concerning abuse by Ukrainian forces. The report said Ukraine had taken some steps to prevent such violations and had cooperated with OHCHR requests, although efforts to ensure accountability remained limited. By contrast, it said Russia had failed to take steps to prevent, investigate or prosecute sexual violence committed by its personnel and had not engaged with OHCHR requests for information. âI am deeply alarmed by the prevalence of these abhorrent acts documented in our report, and fear that they are almost certainly continuing amid the unceasing violence we are witnessing every day in Ukraine,â UN high commissioner for human rights Volker Turk said. title: What's Suwalki gap? Europe's 'achilles heel' that it fears could be Putin's target
text: Polish President Nawrocki and Lithuanian President Nauseda during the military exercise near the Suwalki gap. (File photo/Reuters) Belarusian tanks rolling close to the Polish and Lithuanian border last week, followed almost immediately by Ukraine's biggest strike deep inside Russia, has pushed a little known patch of land back into the spotlight. Barely 100 kilometres long, the Suwalki Gap is the only route by land connecting the three Baltic states (Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia) to the rest of Nato. The European leaders and security officials worry it could become the place where Vladimir Putin chooses to test the alliance without firing the first shot of a full scale war. The gap sits squeezed between Belarus on one side and Kaliningrad on the other, a heavily armed Russian territory, which is not part of the mainland Russia. Kaliningrad, the Russian exclave, was once German land and home to a large German population for centuries, until the Soviet Union took it over after the Nazi army collapsed at the end of the World War II. It was then formally handed to Moscow under the Potsdam Agreement of 1945, signed by the wartime allies as they carved up the map of Europe. It has stayed Russian ever since, cut off from the Russian mainland and sitting right between Poland and Lithuania like a loaded gun pointed at Nato's eastern edge. The Suwalki Gap is the only route by land connecting the three Baltic states. Why the gap is being watched so closely If this narrow corridor were ever blocked or seized, the Baltic states would effectively be sealed off from reinforcement by land. Troops, tanks, fuel and ammunition all rely on this single stretch to move from Poland northwards. That is exactly why Nato treats it as a strategic weak spot, even though there is no solid proof right now that Russia plans to attack it. The Belarusian drills involved mechanised and armoured units training in border defence, counter sabotage work and responses to drones. Minsk called them purely defensive and said their scale stayed below the level requiring advance notice under international agreements, but their location so close to the Suwalki Gap still drew immediate attention from Western capitals. The suspicion compounded after Ukraine's deep strike on Russia, which was also the biggest since 2022 when the war began. A test of nerves? There is, however, no public evidence that Moscow is preparing to seize the corridor or launch a direct attack on Nato territory. The concern lies instead in the possibility of pressure below the threshold of open conflict, including drone incursions, sabotage, cyberattacks and military manoeuvres that could test Nato's ability to distinguish between deliberate aggression and incidents that can be denied or attributed elsewhere. Since Russia's invasion of Ukraine, Nato has strengthened its eastern flank with multinational forces, reinforcement plans and pre-positioned equipment stretching from the Baltic region to southeastern Europe. The measures are intended to ensure that any attempt to disrupt access to the Baltic states can be met quickly and collectively. However, for European security planners, the Suwalki Gap is therefore less a prediction of where the next conflict will begin than a reminder of how it could be its "achilles heel". title: Land victory is the only tangible factor in war: Army chief; says no substitute for self-reliance in weapon development
text: Army chief General Dhiraj Seth NEW DELHI: Amid the continuing Ukraine-Russia war over land boundaries and Iran-US conflict over the control of the Strait of Hormuz, Indian Army chief General Dhiraj Seth said on Sunday that despite modern technological disruptions, physical territorial control remains the ultimate measure of military triumph and âland victory is the only tangible factorâ in war. In his address at NDTV Defence Summit, General Seth said: âWe see salvo after salvo in todayâs social media covering warfare across the globe, where information narratives and warfare are being fired to fog the real battle picture, creating uncertainty and confusion...However, I strongly feel, through all this clutter, one reality that does not change: land will always be the one and only tangible and useful factor of success. Victory was, is, and will always be measured in territorial terms and that territory will be occupied, secured, and defended only by the force.â Gen Seth said technology is certainly shortening battles but it is not necessarily shortening wars, and that âland victory is the only indisputable marker of war victoryâ. âThese millennium wars can best be described as wars with pause. Pause, in fact, is becoming a part of military strategy, with the pause representing not the domination of conflict but merely a change in its intensity and manifestation,â he said. Underlining that there is no substitute for self-reliance, the Army chief said, âAtmanirbharta must be about ensuring that we have the capability to endure without being constrained by what others can or cannot provide. That gives us a good reason to take a hard look at the very pathways of our indigenous capability. Aatmanirbharta must mean design in India, develop in India, manufacture in India, sustain in India, upgrade in India, and also make for the world. â However, Gen Seth advised caution regarding âindigenous obsolescenceâ. âThe challenge is not just to reduce dependencies on others but also to ensure that what we develop indigenously does not become outdated by the time it is dumped. I would like to term it as indigenous obsolescence or that kind of a trap that can get created,â he said. Talking about a photo taken on Dec 16, 1971, that depicted Pakistan surrendering during the Bangladesh war, Gen Seth said: âThe reason I allude to this today is that that photo gave us a very defining moment, because that was the precise moment when the war came to an end. But there is no demarcating moment; there is no termination point which indicates an end to the hostilities.â

title: 70% Swiss say no: Switzerland rejects push for tighter neutrality amid Russia tensions
text: An electoral poster reads âNo war, Yes to Swiss neutralityâ is posted along a road in Epagny, Switzerland (AP) Switzerland has voted against a proposal aimed at tightening the country's long-standing policy of neutrality, with 70 per cent of voters rejecting the measure in a nationwide referendum on Sunday. The proposal was backed by the right-wing Swiss Peopleâs Party, whose supporters argued that Switzerland had moved too close to the European Union and Nato, particularly because of its response to Russiaâs war in Ukraine. The measure was rejected by majorities in all 26 Swiss regions, according to final results released by the Swiss government. What the proposal sought to change The initiative would have restricted Switzerland from joining sanctions against other countries unless those measures had been imposed by the United Nations . That would have significantly affected Switzerlandâs ability to impose sanctions independently. Russia, one of the five permanent members of the UN Security Council, has veto power over decisions by the council. The proposal also sought to limit Switzerlandâs cooperation with military alliances. Switzerland is not a member of NATO, but it has worked with the alliance for around three decades. Under the proposed rules, cooperation with a military alliance would generally have been prohibited unless Switzerland itself faced a threat. Debate over Switzerlandâs neutrality Supporters said the government had moved âdangerously closeâ to the EU and Nato and argued that this could weaken Switzerlandâs security and ability to act independently. The proposal followed Switzerlandâs decision to adopt EU sanctions against Russia after its invasion of Ukraine. Swiss neutrality has been part of the countryâs constitutional framework since the 19th century, but there has been a long-running debate over what neutrality should mean in a changing security environment. Opponents of the proposal argued that the federal government already had enough flexibility to protect Switzerlandâs interests and respond to security threats. Voters divided over security Security concerns featured prominently on both sides of the referendum. Ruth Bolomey, a 65-year-old retiree originally from Hawaii, said she voted for the initiative. âI believe we need neutrality and should keep neutrality for security reasons â for the people.â New York native Jihad Azkoul, 78, voted against the proposal. title: Putin tightens grip on Russian elections with anti-war opposition squeezed out
text: File photo: Russian President Vladimir Putin attends a wreath-laying ceremony at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier by the Kremlin wall in Moscow Russiaâs first parliamentary election since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has begun with voters facing a sharply narrowed political field: the countryâs only openly anti-war party has been barred from running a national list, while pro-Kremlin parties and war veterans dominate the ballot. President Vladimir Putin has cast the election as a demonstration of national unity and support for Russiaâs war in Ukraine. Most anti-war candidates have been excluded, while the ruling United Russia party is expected to retain its dominant position. Yabloko squeezed out of national race The biggest blow to the anti-war camp came in August, when Russiaâs Supreme Court barred liberal Yabloko from fielding a national party list. Yabloko had positioned itself as the countryâs only registered party openly opposing the war and calling for a ceasefire. Some Yabloko candidates are still contesting individual constituencies, but the ruling removed the party from the nationwide contest and left voters with fewer explicitly anti-war choices. The crackdown came after senior Yabloko figures faced prosecution and prison sentences over statements about the war. Party deputy chairman Lev Shlosberg was sentenced to 11 years in prison last month, according to the material cited by Politico. The space left by Yabloko has instead been occupied by parties that formally oppose United Russia on some issues but have backed key Kremlin policies, including the annexation of Ukrainian territories. From war veterans to Putin allies The ballot also features more than 1,000 veterans of Russiaâs war in Ukraine. Their presence reflects the Kremlinâs effort to elevate military veterans as a new political constituency. United Russia's campaign has also brought prominent pro-Kremlin figures into the spotlight. Foreign minister Sergei Lavrov appeared in a campaign advertisement alongside NHL star Alexander Ovechkin and RT chief Margarita Simonyan. Reuters separately reported that Ovechkin appeared in the video after being asked to participate. For the Kremlin, the election is not only about choosing lawmakers but also about demonstrating public support for the war. Putin has urged Russians to vote, saying the result would show that millions stand behind Russian troops and the country's stated wartime goals. Opposition split over âsmart votingâ With anti-war candidates largely squeezed out, parts of the Russian opposition are backing a strategy known as âsmart votingâ â supporting whichever candidate in a constituency is considered most capable of challenging United Russia, even if that candidate belongs to another established party. Yulia Navalnaya, widow of late opposition leader Alexey Navalny, has backed the approach, as has opposition campaigner Maxim Katz. Their argument is that the ballot remains one of the few relatively safe ways for Russians to express dissatisfaction with the Kremlin. But the strategy has divided the opposition itself. Ukraine condemned the voting in Russian-held territories and urged other countries not to recognise the results. The European Union called it a "blatant violation of international law." The liberal Yabloko party, the only registered political entity that openly criticised the war, was removed from the ballot by Russia's Supreme Court last month, although some of its candidates remained in constituency races. Yabloko and the Communist Party also reported that some of their observers were turned away from polling stations and alleged other violations, including ballot boxes being opened after being sealed and voters being denied paper ballots. The claims could not be independently verified. Russia did not invite observers from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe. OSCE Parliamentary Assembly President Pere Joan Pons said the decision breached Russia's commitments as a member of the organisation. Electronic voting in Moscow also came under scrutiny. Election chief Ella Pamfilova said the system had been targeted by cyberattacks. Independent outlet SotaVision reported glitches in electronic registration systems, while Kremlin critic Leonid Volkov urged voters: "Demand a paper ballot!" The election's final day coincided with a major wave of Ukrainian drone attacks. Russia's Defence Ministry said its forces shot down 1,110 Ukrainian drones across Russia, Crimea and the Black Sea. Moscow regional Governor Andrei Vorobyov said two people were killed and 20 wounded. Preliminary election results were expected within hours of voting ending in western Russia.
