title: Putin's party wins again as expected. So why does Russia still hold elections?
text: Why does Russia hold elections if Putin is bound to win Russians went to the polls. The votes were counted. Russian President Putin's party United Russia won again, and comfortably. The result itself was hardly the mystery. The more interesting question is why Russia still goes through the elaborate business of elections when the system makes a genuine change of power extremely unlikely. Because in Russia, an election may not simply be about choosing who governs. It can also tell the Kremlin who is turning up, where support is weakening, which regional leaders can deliver and how well the machinery is working. But first, a simpler question: does a Russian vote actually matter? Putin's ruling United Russia party won 57.83% of the vote, according to Russia's Central Election Commission, with more than 95% of ballots counted. The result gives United Russia 355 of the 450 seats in the State Duma, preserving its constitutional majority. In the previous parliamentary election in 2021, the party officially received 49.8% of the vote. The election was also the first parliamentary vote since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Putin had presented it as a test of support for his policies and the war. The Kremlin said the first parliamentary election since Moscow sent troops to Ukraine in 2022 showed Russians were united around Putin, who has been in power since New Year's Eve 1999. That raises an obvious question: If Russia is widely described as an authoritarian or 'managed' political system, and the Kremlin is not seriously threatened by an opposition party taking power, why bother holding elections at all? Putinâs United Russia party has won 355 of the 450 seats in the State Duma. Does a Russian vote actually matter? It would be too simplistic to say that an individual vote is completely meaningless simply because the ruling party is expected to win. Formally, an individual Russian vote can affect the composition of the Duma in two ways. Half of the 450 seats are distributed through nationwide party-list proportional representation, with a 5% threshold, while the other 225 are elected from single-member constituencies. The weight of an individual vote differs between the two. âIn the party-list contest, one vote is a very small part of the national total, although collectively these votes determine 225 seats and can be particularly important when a party is near the 5% threshold,â explained foreign affairs expert Robinder Sachdev. âIn a close constituency race, however, a relatively small number of votes can directly determine who wins that seat,â explained foreign expert he added. The 2026 result illustrates how strongly the constituency component can amplify a party's parliamentary strength. United Russia won 355 of the 450 seats, up from 343 in the previous Duma and the party's highest total so far. That gives the party well over the two-thirds threshold in the Duma. It can pass ordinary federal legislation without needing support from other parties and has enough votes for federal constitutional laws and the Duma stage of constitutional amendments. âSo an individual vote has limited weight by itself, but aggregated votes â particularly in single-member constituencies â can have a major effect on the parliamentary balance of power,â Sachdev said. Does the vote count actually matter? In the narrowest sense, yes. Russians cast ballots, those ballots are counted and the resulting numbers determine how parliamentary seats are allocated. United Russia's 57.83% vote share is therefore not simply a number that has no connection whatsoever to voting. But whether voters have a meaningful opportunity to change who exercises power is a different question. Russia's political system has placed significant restrictions on genuine electoral competition. Reuters described the 2026 parliamentary election as taking place in a âtightly controlled political systemâ in which candidates opposed to Moscow's war in Ukraine have largely been excluded. Several parties besides United Russia are represented in the Duma, but Russia's parliamentary opposition operates within tightly drawn limits, with the major parties generally supporting Putin on key issues, including the war in Ukraine. According to the Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA), Yabloko, a liberal party that opposed the Ukraine war and called for a ceasefire, was excluded from the federal parliamentary contest. CEPA said Yabloko's support among decided voters had risen to about 6% in the weeks before the election, compared with 1.2% in the 2021 election. Meanwhile, Putin critic Nikolai Bondarenko had already been barred from standing. Putin has been in power since New Year's Eve 1999. So should this be called a gimmick? Not quite. Even when the broad political outcome is predictable, elections can serve several purposes for an authoritarian political system. Sachdev said elections provide formal electoral legitimacy while allowing the leadership to demonstrate a measurable level of public participation and support. âElections also help manage the political system itself,â Sachdev said, adding that they provide opportunities to renew parliament, accommodate different groups within the governing establishment and assess the performance of regional political organisations and officials. They also provide information. âThe Kremlin may already have extensive polling and administrative data, but an actual election reveals the geography, intensity and organisational strength of support across the country,â he said. In other words, the Kremlin does not necessarily need an election to discover who rules Russia. It can use an election to find out how well the political machine is functioning. 1. An election creates a claim of public support The first and most obvious purpose is legitimacy. The Kremlin can point to an electoral result and say that millions of Russians participated and that the governing party received a majority of votes. That does not settle the question of whether the election was free and fair. But politically, the existence of an official vote gives the government a concrete result with which to demonstrate public backing. This election is particularly significant because it took place during the war in Ukraine. The Kremlin has an interest in demonstrating that the war has not produced a political revolt at home. Sachdev said the election allows the Russian leadership to âdemonstrate a measurable level of public participation and supportâ, even if the broader political outcome is predictable. That distinction is important. An election can provide a government with an official measure of participation without necessarily providing an unrestricted contest for political power. 2. It gives the Kremlin a measure of support â even if an imperfect one This is where the question of whether votes âcountâ becomes more complicated. Even in a tightly controlled election, authorities can learn something from participation. How many people turn out? Where is turnout unusually low? Which regions deliver particularly strong support? Where does United Russia perform worse than expected? Are local officials able to mobilise their populations? These are valuable pieces of information for an authoritarian government. A 2021 Carnegie analysis described Russian parliamentary elections as functioning less as contests over who would govern and more as a mechanism for measuring and demonstrating support for Putin's system. Sachdev said an election provides a different kind of information from opinion polls, intelligence reports or administrative data because it âtests behaviour and administrative capacity under real conditions.â âTurnout, abstention, regional variations and the performance of individual candidates can reveal where support is strong, where enthusiasm is weaker, and how effectively governors and local political organisations are able to mobilise voters,â he said. Moreover, information moving upwards through a political hierarchy can be filtered, because officials may have incentives to report favourable results to their superiors. Sachdev said an election can therefore provide an additional dataset against which those reports can be assessed. âPolitical-science research describes this as a âfire alarmâ function of elections,â he said. So the election does not simply measure public opinion. It gives the Kremlin a regional picture of both political sentiment and the effectiveness of the state and party machinery in mobilising voters. Does a Russian vote actually matter? 3. Elections keep political elites in line There is another audience for Russian elections that is often overlooked: the people inside the system. An election allows governors, mayors, party officials and other local power brokers to demonstrate that they can deliver the results expected by Moscow. Carnegie has described regional elections in Russia as an âinitiation ritualâ for governors and local elites â an opportunity for them to demonstrate control over their territories. Sachdev said regional leaders are expected not only to administer their territories but also to maintain political stability and demonstrate an ability to mobilise electoral support. Research on Russian regional politics has found that United Russia has historically performed better where governors command effective political organisations and local networks, he said. This means an election can function almost like an internal performance review. If a governor produces the desired result, it demonstrates political control. If a region suddenly records unexpectedly weak support for the ruling party, that can raise questions in Moscow about the governor's popularity, the effectiveness of the regional administration, the strength of the local party organisation or underlying economic and social dissatisfaction. An unexpectedly poor result would not automatically lead to a governor's removal. But, Sachdev said, electoral underperformance âcan weaken a regional leader's standing with the federal centreâ and become one factor in subsequent decisions about appointments, tenure or political advancement. So even if the Kremlin already knows which party will dominate parliament, the election can tell it how effectively its political network is operating below the national level. 4. It gives voters a controlled way to participate There is also a social function. Russia's government does not necessarily want every citizen to become politically disengaged. Voting gives people a formal mechanism for expressing preferences, even if the range of choices is restricted. The question is not necessarily whether the Kremlin believes Russians are choosing between two equally viable governments. Rather, elections can allow the system to channel political participation without allowing that participation to threaten the basic distribution of power. Sachdev said elections also help ârenew the composition of parliamentâ and accommodate different groups within the governing establishment. This means that even where the election does not pose a serious threat to the ruling political system, it can still play a role in determining which individuals and factions occupy positions within that system. 5. Elections can reveal dissatisfaction â but not necessarily change the government This is perhaps the most counterintuitive part. A controlled election can still contain information about dissatisfaction. People can abstain. They can spoil ballots. They can vote for smaller parties or candidates. They can use whatever limited electoral choices are available to signal disagreement. Russia's political opposition has previously tried to use elections tactically to weaken United Russia, even when it could not realistically replace the Kremlin. But the ability to express dissatisfaction and the ability to translate that dissatisfaction into a change of government are two different things which is why the Kremlin may tolerate a certain degree of electoral competition while drawing firm limits around the political system. So, is the result meaningless? Not necessarily. The official vote count is meaningful as a description of what Russia's electoral authorities say happened. But the number cannot be read in isolation as a straightforward measure of Russians' freely expressed political preferences. The composition of the ballot matters. So does who was permitted to campaign, what political views could be openly expressed, the degree of media access available to competing forces, turnout and the broader electoral environment. This creates the central paradox of Russia's elections - The votes can be real without the contest being genuinely competitive. A Russian voter can make a choice. But the political system determines, to a significant extent, which choices are available in the first place. That is why the 57.83% figure needs to be read carefully. It is an official electoral result, but it is not equivalent to saying that 57.83% of all Russians freely chose Putin's political system. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. title: âArmy of Robotsâ: Ukraine turns to machines for its most dangerous missions
text: Ukraine is unveiling the 'Army of Robots' initiative, focusing on automation for the battlefield (Photo credit: Serhii Mykhalchuk) Ukraine is stepping up its push to bring robots deeper into warfare, with former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov announcing a new âArmy of Robotsâ initiative aimed at developing machines that can take on some of the most dangerous tasks on the battlefield. According to the Kyiv Independent, Fedorov announced the initiative on September 26, describing it as a defence-tech ecosystem that will support the development, testing and deployment of robotic systems for military use. The initiative is intended to build on Ukraineâs experience with drones and expand unmanned warfare from the skies to the ground. Fedorov said the initiative will focus on developing technologies that can reduce soldiersâ exposure to danger, with robots potentially carrying out missions such as reconnaissance, transporting ammunition, evacuating wounded troops, laying and clearing mines, defending positions and conducting strikes. He said the goal is to create a system in which machines can be sent into areas where deploying human soldiers would carry a higher risk, marking a further shift towards unmanned systems in Ukraineâs battlefield strategy. The initiative draws on the model of Ukraineâs âArmy of Dronesâ, which helped accelerate the development and deployment of unmanned aerial systems after Russiaâs full-scale invasion. Fedorovâs plans include the development of humanoid robots capable of carrying out basic battlefield tasks, while other robotic platforms could be used alongside drones for reconnaissance, logistics and combat operations. Robots are already moving into Ukraine's frontline The âArmy of Robotsâ initiative builds on a growing use of unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) by Ukraine's military. According to Ukraine's defence ministry, UGVs carried out more than 25,000 logistics and evacuation missions in August 2026, taking the total number of such missions since the beginning of the year to about 112,000. The systems have been used to deliver ammunition, food and water and evacuate wounded soldiers from high-risk areas. Ukraine's Defence Procurement Agency said more than 22,000 UGVs had been contracted in 2026 by July, nearly twice the number contracted during the whole of 2025. The majority were logistics systems, followed by engineering and combat platforms, with some designed for ammunition delivery, casualty evacuation and reconnaissance-strike missions. Why robots are becoming increasingly important on the battlefield The growing importance of battlefield robots is being driven by the need to keep soldiers away from increasingly dangerous frontline zones. Ukraine's defence ministry says ground robotic systems are being used for logistics, ammunition delivery, casualty evacuation and other missions without putting personnel directly into strike zones. Reuters reported earlier this month that Ukrainian units are increasingly deploying UGVs to carry explosives, transport supplies and evacuate wounded troops, with commanders viewing them as a way to reduce human casualties while increasing operational flexibility. Nato's research identifies reducing casualties, lowering manpower requirements and improving operational effectiveness among the main drivers behind the adoption of robotic and autonomous systems. The US Army is also expanding the use of unmanned systems, saying they can increase lethality while reducing risk to soldiers

title: India unlikely to face major food, fertiliser crisis despite global headwinds: Finance Commission chairman
text: "Looking at the overall market, I do not think we are heading towards a crisis," Finance Commission chairman said (Photo: ANI). NEW DELHI: India is unlikely to face a major food or fertiliser crisis, despite ongoing global conflicts, the Finance Commission chairman said on Saturday. Speaking to news agency ANI, 16th Finance Commission chairman Arvind Panagariya said the country has bolstered its fertiliser supplies and shown that it can withstand recent energy shocks. Earlier this week, foreign minister S Jaishankar said that the Ukraine and West Asia conflicts were affecting grain exports and fertiliser production, while energy costs and tighter financial conditions were adding further strain on developing economies. "If we look at our recent experience with the war in West Asia and the way we were able to handle the energy side, I do not think there is anything here that we need to fear very seriously," Panagariya said. He noted that India's fertiliser position had strengthened, partly because domestic plants had been restarted, and that supplies could also be obtained from other countries. "There is supply, and fertilisers can also be purchased from other countries," he said. He added that although the West Asia conflict had created uncertainty, the large energy shock that had been feared had not materialised for India. The government has also stated that it has kept fertiliser availability adequate in spite of West Asia-related supply disruptions, through domestic production, diversified imports and advance stocking. According to Panagariya, India had succeeded in limiting the impact of the energy shock on households, although commercial LPG users, such as restaurants and hotels, faced some temporary pressure. "We were able to absorb this shock quite well. Going forward, I believe our ability to absorb such shocks will increase, not decrease," he said. According to the chairman, disruption to supplies from major producers such as Ukraine could, in fact, increase demand for certain Indian exports. "If the war leads to lower supplies from Ukraine, demand for our food products could increase," he said. "If that pushes prices higher, our exporters would benefit." title: Nato boosts intelligence-sharing as Russia-linked sabotage fears grow in Europe
text: Russia-linked sabotage puts Nato on alert as Europe takes bigger security role (representative image) Nato is stepping up intelligence-sharing in response to a series of sabotage and other incidents apparently linked to Russia, while the alliance remains prepared to deal with potential threats from Moscow, its top military commander said on Thursday. US Air Force General Alexus Grynkewich, Nato's Supreme Allied Commander Europe, told Reuters that the recent incidents were concerning but said the alliance had the capabilities and mechanisms needed to manage the risks. The comments came after Denmark's defence intelligence service warned that Russia was likely to intensify its hybrid warfare campaign against Western countries in the coming months. The assessment also said there was a "low but growing risk" that Moscow could launch a limited military attack against one or more Nato countries bordering Russia. Nato says limited attack remains unlikely Grynkewich referred to several incidents in recent weeks, including an attempted drone attack at Germany's Leipzig/Halle Airport and an incident involving a Russian ship that fired flares towards a Danish military helicopter. "It's concerning," Grynkewich told Reuters, but added that Nato should be "calm and confident" because it had the tools and mechanisms required to manage the risk. Asked about the possibility of a limited Russian attack on Nato territory, Grynkewich described such a development as "unlikely but something that we can't rule out". He also rejected suggestions that Russian President Vladimir Putin could see an opportunity to attack Nato because the US had used much of its stockpile of highly accurate long-range missiles during the war with Iran. "Absolutely not. He better not try it on my watch," Grynkewich said, adding that Nato was well positioned to defend its territory. He said he was confident he had the necessary authorities to take action to deter aggression against the alliance if emerging threats were detected. Russia has repeatedly denied involvement in hybrid warfare or sabotage operations in Nato countries, as well as allegations that it is planning a confrontation with the alliance. Denmark warns of more hybrid attacks Denmark's Defence Intelligence Service said Russia was likely to step up its hybrid campaign, which includes sabotage, cyberattacks, disinformation and other hostile activities below the level of conventional warfare. The agency said this could include destructive cyberattacks capable of disrupting critical societal functions and sabotage attacks carrying a high risk of casualties. It also said Russia had become "more willing to take risks". The assessment said there was a "low but growing risk" of a limited Russian military attack against one or more Nato countries bordering Russia, potentially in the coming months. However, it said there were no indications that Russia would launch an outright invasion of one or more Nato countries. The agency said such actions could seek to divert European resources from supporting Ukraine and create divisions within Nato. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk also warned last week that Russia was planning hybrid strikes involving drones or rockets against European countries supporting Ukraine, including Poland. He said Moscow could present such attacks as accidental. Nato secretary-general Mark Rutte said the alliance had action plans to respond to sabotage and drone incidents. He said, "All the response options are there, and we will use whatever we need." US ambassador to Nato Matthew Whitaker, however, cautioned against overreacting to the incidents. He said the current volume of activity did not indicate that a conflict was imminent and added, "We haven't reached that threshold." European allies set to take greater role The warnings come as Nato undergoes a broader reshuffle, with European countries taking greater responsibility for their own security in line with US President Donald Trump's demands. A European commander is set to take over Nato's Joint Force Command Norfolk, which oversees operations in the Arctic and northern Europe and the protection of transatlantic resupply routes. A European official will also take charge of Nato's Joint Force Command in Naples. Grynkewich said the US would continue to provide "critical but more limited capabilities" as European allies assumed a greater role. He said there was "no predetermined outcome" regarding the number of US troops that would remain in Europe or which capabilities might be relocated. About 80,000 US troops are currently based on the continent.

title: Russia backs India's claim to UNSC seat, firmly shuts door on Germany & Japan
text: Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov addresses the 81st United Nations General Assembly (Photo: Reuters). Russia on Saturday backed a permanent seat for India and Brazil on the United Nations Security Council, while strongly opposing the same for Western countries. During his speech at the General Assembly, Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov said no additional seats at the UNSC should be given to Western countries, especially to Germany and the US ally, Japan. Moscow has repeatedly backed Indiaâs candidature as part of a broader push to make the Council more representative of Asia, Africa and Latin America. Lavrov has previously argued that the current composition no longer reflects todayâs global balance and explicitly endorsed India, alongside Brazil, for permanent membership. This support was reiterated in the 2026 BRICS New Delhi Declaration, with China and Russia backing India and Brazil for a greater role in the UN, including the Security Council. Lavrov accused the West of continuously pumping weapons into Ukraine while helping target drones and missiles at Russia's civilians and civilian infrastructure. He also mentioned that Europe raised an anti-Moscow regime in Kyivv, in order to control the Russian influence. "To pursue a utopian goal of containing Russia, the West dismantled the European security system and cultivated a Russophobic regime in Kyiv," he said, while warning the Western nations of "consequences". He further accused Europe of doing everything to block a peaceful settlement with Ukraine and disrupt negotiation prospects favoured by many, including the Trump administration.
